frames.text: Pneumonia (PNA) on CXR: whiter
PNA: dull percussion note
Lobar PNA: ↓ chest movement on affected side
Consolidation: ↑ fremitus, dull, bronchial sounds
Pneumonia: crackles over the involved lobe

q: Which percussion note is expected over an area of pneumonia?
e: Dull or flat notes occur over increased tissue density or fluid, as in pneumonia. Hyperresonance suggests hyperinflation or pneumothorax.

q: On a chest X-ray, which finding appears whiter (radiopaque)?
e: Whiter: atelectasis, consolidation/pneumonia, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion. Darker (more air): emphysema, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum.

q: Which exam finding goes with consolidation?
o: Increased vocal fremitus with dull percussion
Trachea shifted away with absent breath sounds
e: Consolidation gives increased vocal fremitus, dull percussion, and bronchial breath sounds/crackles.

frames.text: Pleural effusion: blunted costophrenic angle
Pleural effusion on CXR: whiter
Effusion exam: trachea away, dull, absent BS
Effusion must be substantial to shift trachea
Effusion causes: CHF, malignancy, PNA, PE

q: A chest X-ray shows a blunted costophrenic angle. What should you think of?
e: Blunted costophrenic angle suggests pleural effusion; flattened diaphragm suggests hyperinflation; elevated diaphragm suggests volume loss or diaphragm weakness.

q: Which exam finding fits a large pleural effusion rather than atelectasis?
e: Pleural effusion: trachea away. Atelectasis: trachea toward.

q: Which condition is listed as a cause of pleural effusion?
e: Pleural effusions may be caused by CHF, malignancy, pneumonia, and pulmonary embolism.

frames.text: Accessory muscle use at rest = ↑ WOB
Seen in emphysema and any ↑ WOB
Accessory muscles: ↑ WOB or diaphragm weakness
Inspiratory accessory muscles (Hess)

q: Accessory muscle use in a resting patient mainly signals:
e: Accessory muscle use at rest = increased WOB.

q: Which muscle is an accessory muscle of inspiration?
e: Hess lists the scalene, sternocleidomastoid, pectoralis major, trapezius, and external intercostals as accessory muscles of inspiration; rectus abdominis, internal intercostals and transverse abdominis are expiratory.

frames.text: NIF: normal > -60; vent pts need -20 to extubate
SBT passed: full 30–120 min, consider extubation
SBT pass ≠ automatic extubation
NHLBI protocol: tolerated ≥ 30 min → consider extubation
NHLBI SBT distress = two or more signs

q: What is the minimum NIF (MIP) listed for a ventilated patient to be successfully extubated?
e: Normal NIF is > -60; need a minimum of -20 on vent pts to be successfully extubated. -40 is the COPD value.

q: Under the NHLBI ARDS protocol, after how long of a tolerated SBT do you consider extubation?
e: If tolerated for at least 30 minutes, consider extubation.

q: A patient passes an SBT. What do the course notes say about extubation?
o: Consider extubation readiness; weaning readiness is not extubation readiness
Extubation is contraindicated until NIF is -60
e: Passing an SBT means you consider extubation; the notes stress that weaning readiness is not extubation readiness.

frames.text: Extubation: upright, suction, 100% O2
Cough with suction, pull the tube
After: cool humidified O2, higher FIO2
Stridor: cool aerosol O2 + racemic epi
Worst complication: laryngospasm; NPO 24 h

q: What is the most serious complication that can occur with extubation?
e: Most serious complication that can occur with Extubation is Laryngospasm.

q: After extubation, the O2 should be given at what FIO2 relative to before extubation?
e: Provide cool, humidified O2 via aerosol mask or a nasal cannula at a higher FIO2 than prior to extubation.

q: Stridor develops after extubation. What does the source recommend?
o: Cool humidified O2 by aerosol mask and recommend aerosolized racemic epinephrine
e: If stridor develops, provide cool, humidified O2 via aerosol mask, and recommend treatment with aerosolized Racemic Epinephrine.

frames.text: Best weaning indicators: RR and RSBI
RSBI = f ÷ VT (L)
RSBI < 105 favorable; > 105 failure likely
Critical minimum VC ≈ 1 L (15 mL/kg)

q: Which RSBI value is favorable for weaning?
e: <105 = favorable for weaning; >105 = increased likelihood of weaning failure.

q: How is the RSBI computed?
o: Breathing rate ÷ average VT in liters
Average VT in liters ÷ breathing rate
e: RSBI = f ÷ VT (L).

q: Which measures does the course slide call the best indicators that a patient can tolerate spontaneous breathing?
e: RR and RSBI are the best indicators; MIP/NIF and VC are less frequently obtained.

frames.text: NHLBI SBT readiness: FiO2 ≤ 0.40 + PEEP ≤ 8, or FiO2 ≤ 0.50 + PEEP ≤ 5
Also: SBP ≥ 90 off pressors, no NM blockade
Tolerance: SpO2 ≥ 90% and/or PaO2 ≥ 60; VT ≥ 4 mL/kg PBW
Tolerance: RR ≤ 35/min, pH ≥ 7.30, no distress
Not tolerated → resume pre-weaning settings

q: Under the NHLBI ARDS protocol, which FiO2/PEEP combination meets the criteria for SBT readiness?
e: Readiness: FiO2 ≤ 0.40 and PEEP ≤ 8 cm H2O, or FiO2 ≤ 0.50 and PEEP ≤ 5 cm H2O.

q: What is the minimum spontaneous VT listed for tolerating the NHLBI SBT?
e: Tolerance criteria include spontaneous VT ≥ 4 mL/kg PBW, RR ≤ 35/min, and SpO2 ≥ 90% and/or PaO2 ≥ 60 torr.

q: A patient does not tolerate the NHLBI SBT. What does the protocol say to do?
e: If not tolerated, resume pre-weaning settings.

frames.text: Cardiomegaly: CT ratio > 50% on a PA CXR
AP film magnifies the heart
Heart failure: big heart, congestion, ± effusions
ETT tip: 4–6 cm above the carina
Too deep → right mainstem; too high → extubation risk

q: On a PA chest X-ray, cardiomegaly exists when the cardiothoracic (CT) ratio exceeds:
e: Cardiomegaly exists when the CT ratio exceeds 50% on a PA CXR; normally the heart width is less than 50% of the thoracic cage.

q: Where should the ETT tip ideally sit on the chest X-ray?
o: In the pharynx, above the vocal cords
e: Ideally, the ETT tip should be positioned 4–6 cm above the carina. Too deep usually enters the right mainstem bronchus.

frames.text: PNA on CXR: segmental or lobar opacities
PNA vs atelectasis: lung volume preserved
PNA: air bronchograms ± pleural effusions
Air bronchogram → opacity is pulmonary
Silhouette sign: finds the affected lobe

q: Per Hess, which chest X-ray feature distinguishes pneumonia from atelectasis?
o: Lung volume is preserved in pneumonia
Pneumonia shifts the fissures toward the lesion
e: In pneumonia, as opposed to atelectasis, lung volume is preserved and findings persist for days to weeks. Hemidiaphragm elevation and fissure displacement are atelectasis signs.

q: An air bronchogram on chest X-ray indicates that the underlying opacity is of what origin?
e: An air bronchogram indicates that the underlying opacity is of pulmonary (rather than pleural or mediastinal) origin.

frames.text: Flattened diaphragm → hyperinflation
Elevated diaphragm → volume loss or weakness
Darker (radiolucent): emphysema, pneumothorax
CXR quality: R-I-P-E
Underexposed = too white; overexposed = too dark

q: A chest X-ray shows flattened diaphragms. What should you think of?
e: Flattened diaphragm → think hyperinflation. Elevated diaphragm → think volume loss or diaphragm weakness (atelectasis, phrenic nerve paralysis).

frames.text: Hess: ready when intubation cause corrected + criteria met
Protect airway, clear secretions, secretion load, upper airway
Cough peak flow ≤ 60 L/min: nearly 5× likely to fail
Secretions > 2.5 mL/h: 3× likely to fail
Can't do 4 simple tasks: > 4× likely to fail

q: Per Hess, a cough peak flow at what level made extubation failure nearly five times as likely?
e: Patients with a cough peak flow of 60 L/min or less were nearly five times as likely to fail extubation.

q: Per Hess, which secretion finding made extubation failure three times as likely?
o: Secretions cleared by a strong cough
e: Patients with secretions of more than 2.5 mL/h are three times as likely to fail.

frames.text: Cuff leak test: deflate cuff, assess for leak
Quantitative: leak volume or % of VT
Controversial: false positives and negatives
Reserve for high risk of post-extubation stridor

q: Per Hess, the cuff leak test should be reserved for which patients?
o: Those at high risk of post-extubation stridor
Patients with no upper-airway risk factors
e: The cuff leak test should be reserved for patients at high risk of post-extubation stridor; its value is controversial because false positives and false negatives are common.

frames.text: A % solution = grams per 100 mL
Shortcut: Drug % × 10 = mg/mL

q: Using the handout shortcut, what is the concentration of a 0.5% albuterol solution?
e: Drug % × 10 = mg/mL, so 0.5% × 10 = 5 mg/mL.

q: What is the ALWAYS first step in a percent-solution dose calculation?
e: First step is ALWAYS convert the % (concentration) solution: Drug % × 10 = mg/mL.

frames.text: Step 1: convert % → mg/mL
Step 2: multiply by volume given
Example: 3 mL of 0.083% albuterol
Percent = concentration; × volume = dose

q: How many mg of albuterol are in 3 mL of a 0.083% solution?
After converting % to mg/mL, how do you get the actual drug dose?
e: Step 2: multiply by volume given - tells you actual drug dose.

frames.text: Dose ordered ÷ concentration = volume
Example: 2.5 mg from 5 mg/mL
Sense check: half the dose = half the volume
2.5 mg vial ≈ 0.5 mL of 0.5% solution

q: How many mL of a 0.5% albuterol solution contain a 2.5 mg dose?
e: 0.5% × 10 = 5 mg/mL; 2.5 mg is half of 5 mg, so about half the volume (0.5 mL).

q: To find the volume to give for an ordered dose, you:
o: Divide the dose by the concentration
Multiply the dose by the concentration
Divide the concentration by the dose
Add the diluent to the dose
e: Dose ordered ÷ Concentration equals volume.

frames.text: Diluent does NOT change the drug dose
Saline only changes total volume and treatment time
2.5 mg is 2.5 mg with 2, 5, or 10 mL saline
Aim for about 2.5–3 mL total volume
Why add diluent: most nebs need ≥ ~1 mL

q: What does adding saline to a nebulizer change?
o: Only the total volume and how long the treatment takes
e: Adding saline does NOT reduce the drug dose. It only increases the total liquid volume and affects how long the treatment lasts: same dose, same medication effect.

q: 2.5 mg of albuterol is mixed with 10 mL of saline. How much albuterol is delivered?
e: You get 2.5 mg whether it is mixed with 2, 5, or 10 mL of saline.

frames.text: mL = cc
4,500 mg = 4.5 grams
Proportions: use consistent units
Write it out

q: 4,500 mg equals how many grams?
e: 4,500 mg = 4.5 grams, because 1,000 mg = 1 g.

q: How does a milliliter (mL) compare with a cubic centimeter (cc)?
o: They are exactly the same volume
e: A milliliter (mL) and a cubic centimeter (cc) are exactly the same volume.

frames.text: 1 teaspoon = 5 mL = 60 gtts
1 tablespoon = 15 mL (3 teaspoons)
1 cup = 240 mL (8 fl oz)
% preparations: w/w, w/v, v/v
Solute dissolves; solvent does the dissolving

q: 1 teaspoon equals how many mL?
e: 1 teaspoon = 5 mL = 60 drops (gtts); 1 tablespoon = 15 mL (3 teaspoons).

q: In a solution, the solute is:
o: The substance that does the dissolving
e: Solute: the substance that gets dissolved. Solvent: the substance that does the dissolving.

frames.text: ABG goals: normalize pH, oxygenate, optimize PEEP
pH problem → adjust minute ventilation
pH goal 7.35–7.45
May allow pH 7.25 to 7.50
↑ VE → ↓ PaCO2; ↓ VE → ↑ PaCO2

q: After an ABG shows an abnormal pH, which ventilator-related variable do you adjust to normalize it?
e: To normalize the pH, you adjust the minute ventilation, which alters the PaCO2.

q: Hess: what happens to PaCO2 when minute ventilation increases?
e: An increase in minute ventilation decreases PaCO2, and a decrease in minute ventilation increases PaCO2.

q: A COPD patient with chronic CO2 retention can have a normal pH at what PaCO2?
e: In a COPD patient with chronic CO2 retention (compensated respiratory acidosis), a normal pH may be achieved with PaCO2 levels of 55 torr or higher.

frames.text: Fix pH: adjust rate first (12–24/min)
Rate alone not enough → alter delivered VT
VT 4–8 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤ 30–35
PC modes: change ΔP to change VT
pH < 7.30 at limits → permissive hypercapnia

q: In most modes, what do you adjust first to correct the pH?
e: In most modes, to adjust the pH, you first adjust the set rate.

q: Rate changes alone did not normalize the pH. What is the next step?
e: If rate adjustments alone do not normalize the pH, then you alter the delivered VT.

q: In pressure control, how do you alter the delivered VT?
o: Change the driving pressure (ΔP = PIP – PEEP)
e: In PC modes, alter the delivered VT by increasing or decreasing the Driving Pressure, ΔP (PIP – PEEP).

q: pH remains below 7.30 while rate, VT, and Pplat are at recommended high limits. What should you consider?
e: Consider Permissive Hypercapnia (allowing the PaCO2 to rise as long as the pH remains above 7.20–7.25).

q: What is the recommended upper limit for Pplat when adjusting delivered VT?
e: Try to keep VT between 4–8 mL/kg PBW with the Pplat ≤ 30–35 cm H2O.

frames.text: Oxygenation: PaO2/SaO2, Hb, circulation
Can keep PaO2 on < 50% O2 → change FiO2
Cannot on < 50% O2 → change PEEP
PaO2/FiO2 ≤ 200 → NHLBI ARDS protocol
Improving: FiO2 down to ≤ 50%, then PEEP

q: An acceptable PaO2/SaO2 can be maintained on less than 50% O2. How do you normalize oxygenation?
e: If an acceptable PaO2/SaO2 can be maintained on less than 50% O2, normalize oxygenation by altering the FiO2.

q: When oxygenation improves, what do you decrease first?
o: FiO2 until it is 50% or less
e: When oxygenation improves, first decrease FiO2 until it is 50% or less, then lower PEEP.

q: Which minimum Hb content is listed when checking oxygenation?
e: Check and confirm an acceptable Hb content (≥10 g/dL).

frames.text: Too little PEEP vs too much PEEP
Optimal PEEP: max benefit, min risk
PEEP to keep SpO2 ≥ 88–90% without ↓ BP
Method: highest static compliance

q: Too much PEEP can cause:
e: Too little PEEP may not prevent alveolar collapse, whereas too much can cause overdistension and worsen preexisting lung injury.

q: A practical definition of optimal PEEP is the level needed to maintain SpO2 of at least 88–90% while:
e: The PEEP needed to maintain SpO2 ≥ 88-90% WITHOUT lowering the pt’s BP.

frames.text: Vesicular: peripheral lung fields
Bronchial: over the trachea
Bronchovesicular: upper sternum / between scapulae
Hess: bronchovesicular = bronchi/alveoli junction
Normal sound in wrong place = abnormal

q: Which normal breath sound is heard over the peripheral lung fields?
e: Vesicular → peripheral lung fields; bronchial → trachea.

q: Bronchial breath sounds heard in the lung periphery or bases suggest:
e: Bronchial breath sounds heard over the periphery or in the bases of the lungs suggest consolidation of lung tissue.

q: According to the course slides, bronchovesicular sounds are normally heard at the:
e: Bronchovesicular → upper sternum / between scapulae. Bronchial → trachea.

frames.text: Adventitious BS: rhonchi, wheezes, crackles, stridor
Crackles → airway/alveolar opening or secretions
Crackle cause: terminal airways pop open
Crackles: late inspiration, fine, high-pitched
Common with congestive heart failure

q: What causes crackles (per Hess)?
o: Terminal airways popping open late in inspiration with fluid or secretions
e: Crackles result when the terminal airways pop open late in inspiration because fluid or secretions have accumulated.

q: Crackles are usually heard:
o: At the end of inspiration, over the bases
Only on expiration, over the trachea
e: Usually heard at the end of inspiration, fine and high pitched; crackles are heard most often over the lung bases.

frames.text: Rhonchi → secretions/mucus; may clear with cough
Rhonchi: deeper, rumbling, louder on expiration
Cause: thick secretions, spasm, or tumor
Rhonchi: low-pitched, snoring-like

q: Which sound is described as low-pitched, snoring-like, from larger airways with secretions?
e: Rhonchi are low-pitched and snoring-like; wheezes are high-pitched and musical.

q: Which sound may clear after the patient coughs?
e: Rhonchi → secretions/mucus; may clear with coughing.

frames.text: Wheezes → narrowed/obstructed airways
Wheeze: musical, from narrowed airways
Sibilant wheezes: mostly on expiration
Notes: high-pitched, small airways; Hess: high or low

q: Wheezes are caused by air passing through:
e: Wheezes → narrowed/obstructed airways; caused by air passing through narrowed airways, such as bronchospasm of asthma.

q: When are sibilant wheezes most often heard?
e: Most often, sibilant wheezes are heard on expiration.

frames.text: Stridor → upper-airway obstruction
Stridor: crowing; larynx/trachea edema
Can occur after extubation
Croup in children: barking cough

q: Stridor indicates:
e: Stridor → upper-airway obstruction.

q: Which sound is a crowing sound commonly caused by inflammation and edema of the larynx and trachea?
e: Stridor is a crowing sound commonly caused by inflammation and edema of the larynx and trachea.

frames.text: Pleural friction rub → inflamed pleural surfaces
Rub: grating, like leather on leather
Cause: inflamed pleurae no longer glide silently
Localized to the area of pleural irritation

q: A continuous grating sound like two pieces of leather rubbing is a:
e: A pleural friction rub is a continuous grating sound like that heard when two pieces of leather rub together.

q: What produces a pleural friction rub?
o: Inflamed visceral and parietal pleurae no longer gliding silently
e: This sound is produced when the visceral and parietal pleurae become inflamed and no longer glide silently against each other.

frames.text: Diminished BS: shallow or slow breathing
Also obstruction or hyperinflation
Pleural air/fluid and obesity

q: Which of these can decrease breath sounds?
o: Bronchial sounds heard over the trachea
Vesicular sounds heard over the periphery
e: Air or fluid in the pleural space and obesity can reduce BS; BS are diminished when breathing is shallow or slow. Bronchial over the trachea and vesicular over the periphery are normal.

q: Which list contains only adventitious breath sounds?
e: Adventitious (abnormal) BS include rhonchi, wheezes, crackles (rales), and stridor.

frames.text: Grunting: newborns in respiratory distress
Grunting cause: glottis closed to keep lung volume
Consolidation voice sounds
Egophony: e sounds like a

q: Grunting in a newborn with respiratory distress occurs when:
o: The glottis is closed in an attempt to maintain lung volume
Terminal airways pop open late in inspiration
The larynx is swollen from croup
e: Grunting is a sound heard in newborns with respiratory distress. It occurs when the glottis is closed in an attempt to maintain lung volume.

q: When the patient says “e,” you hear “a” over an area of lung. This egophony suggests:
e: Over consolidated areas, the letter e converts to the sound of the letter a (the e to a phenomenon); voice sounds are typical of consolidation.

frames.text: Orthopnea: uncomfortable lying down, relieved sitting/standing
Dyspnea vs orthopnea
Hess: orthopnea = must sit or stand to breathe
Platypnea is the opposite: breathing only lying flat

q: Orthopnea is breathlessness that:
o: Occurs lying down and is relieved by sitting or standing
Occurs sitting up and is relieved by lying flat
Occurs several hours after lying down, suddenly
e: Orthopnea is uncomfortable breathing when lying down, typically relieved by sitting or standing up.

q: Which term means difficulty breathing unless lying flat?
e: Hess: platypnea is difficulty in breathing unless lying flat; orthopnea means the person must sit or stand to breathe.

frames.text: Kussmaul → metabolic acidosis / DKA
Kussmaul = compensatory hyperventilation
Rapid rate + higher-than-normal tidal volume
Renal-failure acidosis: Kussmaul to blow off CO₂
Kussmaul: regular rhythm, no apnea

q: Kussmaul breathing is a compensation for:
e: Kussmaul breathing → metabolic acidosis/DKA.

q: Which pattern is a rapid rate with higher-than-normal tidal volume?
e: Kussmaul breathing is characterized by a rapid respiratory rate and a higher than normal tidal volume.

frames.text: Cheyne-Stokes: slow, shallow → faster, deeper
Crescendo–decrescendo, then apnea
Seen with cerebral vascular disease and CHF
May be normal in young children and elderly
Clinical Data deck: wax and wane with apnea; CHF, stroke

q: Which breathing pattern is a crescendo–decrescendo pattern followed by periods of apnea?
e: Cheyne-Stokes: slow, shallow breaths that rapidly increase in depth and rate, a crescendo–decrescendo pattern followed by apnea.

q: Cheyne-Stokes breathing is seen in:
o: Cerebral vascular disease and congestive heart failure
e: Cheyne-Stokes occurs in cerebral vascular disease and congestive heart failure; Kussmaul in DKA; Biot in elevated intracranial pressure and meningitis.

frames.text: Biot: ↑ ICP and meningitis
Short bursts of uniform deep breaths, then apnea
Other course deck: irregular, equal VT, then apnea
Linked to CNS injury, ↑ ICP, brainstem damage

q: Biot respirations are symptomatic of:
e: Biot respirations are symptomatic of elevated intracranial pressure and meningitis.

q: How long are the apneic periods in Biot respirations (Hess)?
e: A short burst of uniform, deep respirations, followed by periods of apnea lasting 10 to 30 seconds.

q: A patient has a short burst of uniform, deep breaths followed by apnea, with elevated ICP. This is:
e: Biot respirations: short burst of uniform, deep respirations followed by apnea; symptomatic of elevated intracranial pressure.

q: Unlike Cheyne-Stokes breathing, Kussmaul respirations have:
o: A regular rhythm without periods of apnea
A crescendo–decrescendo pattern followed by apnea
Short bursts of deep breaths followed by apnea
e: Kussmaul respirations have a regular rhythm without periods of apnea; Cheyne-Stokes is a crescendo–decrescendo pattern followed by apnea.

frames.text: Vane respirometer: vane + gears + dial
Volume device; accurate within 2% of its flow range
Unidirectional: inlet to outlet
Overreads at high flow, underreads at low flow
NEVER use for forced maneuvers

q: A vane-type (Wright) respirometer tends to:
o: Overread at high flows and underread at low flows
Underread at high flows and overread at low flows
e: Like any turbine system, these devices tend to overread at high flows and underread at low flows.

q: Why shouldn't a mechanical vane respirometer measure forced vital capacity maneuvers?
o: Flows outside its range can damage it
e: They are easily damaged by flows outside their recommended range, so they should never be used to measure forced flows or volumes.

q: A mechanical vane respirometer measures flow in which direction?
e: Measurements made with these devices are unidirectional, always being from device inlet to outlet.

frames.text: Wright respirometer + one-way valve
VT = VE ÷ f
Normal use: expiratory volumes
Inspiratory volume: reverse the setup
Wright = unidirectional: inlet toward the flow

q: For its normal use, the Wright respirometer measures which volumes?
e: The respirometer is positioned to measure Expiratory Volumes (its normal use), inlet on the expiratory side of the breathing valve.

q: How do you compute VT from the minute ventilation and breath rate?
e: To compute the VT, you divide the minute ventilation by the frequency (VT = VE ÷ f).

frames.text: Peak flow meter measures PEFR
PEFR = maximum flow on forced expiration
Simple measure of airway obstruction
Effort dependent: monitoring, not diagnosis
Uses: bronchodilator response, asthma severity

q: Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) is best described as a:
o: Monitoring tool, not used for diagnosis
e: Because the PEFR is highly effort dependent, it is not used for diagnosis, but instead is considered a monitoring tool.

q: Which instrument measures peak expiratory flow?
e: PEF/PEFR is a person's maximum speed of expiration, as measured with a peak flow meter.

frames.text: MIP/NIF is measured with a manometer
Needs an alert, cooperative patient
Valve flipped for MIP vs MEP
Cough-assist manometer reads cm H2O
Neonatal bag-mask: in-line manometer for PIP and PEEP

q: What device is used to measure MIP (NIF)?
o: A manometer on a one-way valve allowing exhalation but not inspiration
e: Measure the MIP using a manometer attached to a one-way valve configured to allow exhalation but not inspiration.

q: MIP and MEP can only be measured on which patients?
e: You can only measure MIP and MEP on an alert and cooperative patient.

frames.text: Capnometer = device taking the readings
Capnogram = the waveform
Capnometry = numeric CO2 display
Capnography = CO2 plotted as a waveform
Most capnometers use infrared absorption

q: The capnogram is:
e: Capnogram: the waveform. Capnograph or capnometer: the device that takes the readings.

q: Most capnometers measure CO2 by:
e: Most capnometers measure CO2 by infrared absorption, although mass spectrometry and Raman spectrometry can also be used.

frames.text: 3-L syringe: checks spirometer volume
Daily calibration check
Low volume → leak; high → setup/BTPS

q: The course slides give what acceptable range for a 3.00 L calibration syringe?
e: 3.00 L ± 0.09 L = acceptable range of 2.91–3.09 L (± 3% or ± 50 mL, whichever is larger). Hess uses ±3.5%.

q: A 3-L syringe check reads low (< 2.91 L). What should you do first?
e: If you obtain a low volume (< 2.91 L), first repeat the leak check. Low volume: think leak.

q: A 3-L syringe check reads high (> 3.09 L). What should you verify?
o: BTPS correction is OFF and syringe/spirometer temperatures match
e: If high (> 3.09 L), recheck zeroing, make sure BTPS correction is OFF, and confirm that temperatures of the syringe and spirometer are the same.

q: How often is a calibration check with a 3-L syringe required (Hess)?
o: Only when a new patient is tested
e: A calibration check using a 3-L syringe is required daily.

frames.text: 3-L syringe: calibration with BTPS OFF
Flow check: 3-L syringe at 3 speeds
Linearity: within 100 mL of 3.0 L

q: During spirometer calibration with the 3-L syringe, BTPS correction should be:
e: Calibration syringe → BTPS correction OFF; patient spirometry → BTPS correction ON.

frames.text: SD range for QC: ±2 SD
Within limits = in control
Outside limits = analytical error
PFT biological controls: outside 2 SD
PFT repeatability: top 2 FVC & FEV1 within 150 mL

q: What are the Levy-Jennings chart bounding limits?
e: Bounding limits are set to within ±2 SD.

q: Control measurements fall outside the Levy-Jennings bounding limits. This indicates:
e: Control measurements that fall outside the bounding limits indicate “analytical error”.

frames.text: Z score = (measured − predicted) ÷ residual SD
Z = –1.64 is the LLN; +1.64 is the ULN
Slides: normal = 80–120% of predicted
Hess: “80% of predicted” rule is invalid

q: Per Hess, what Z score marks the lower limit of normal (LLN) for a PFT value?
e: The predicted Z score is zero; a Z score of –1.64 is the LLN and +1.64 is the ULN.

q: In a normal (bell-shaped) distribution, ±2 SD encompasses about what percent of values?
e: ±1 SD includes 68% of the values, ±2 SD encompasses 95%, and ±3 SD encompasses 99%.

frames.text: Trachea: toward volume loss / away from pressure
Toward: atelectasis, fibrosis, surgical resection
Away: pneumothorax, large effusion, large mass
PTX shift usually means large/tension PTX

q: A patient has atelectasis of the right lung. Which way does the trachea shift?
o: Only if a tension pneumothorax is also present
e: Trachea: toward volume loss / away from pressure. Atelectasis causes the trachea to be deviated toward the affected side.

q: Which condition pushes the trachea AWAY from the affected side?
e: Away from space-occupying pathologies: pneumothorax, large pleural effusion, large mass. Atelectasis, fibrosis, and resection pull it toward.

frames.text: Paradoxical: wall moves IN on inhale, OUT on exhale
A sign of respiratory distress / high WOB
Abdomen IN on inspiration → diaphragm weakness
Chest wall IN on inspiration → chest wall muscle paralysis

q: In paradoxical breathing, what does the chest or abdominal wall do when the patient takes a breath in?
o: Moves out, as in normal breathing
e: The chest wall or abdominal wall moves in when taking a breath and out when exhaling, the opposite of normal breathing movement.

q: Per Hess, paradoxical inward movement of the ABDOMEN during inspiration indicates:
o: Paralysis of the chest wall muscles
e: Hess: abdominal paradox on inspiration indicates diaphragm weakness or paralysis. Chest-wall paradox indicates chest wall muscle paralysis; flail chest is a chest wall moving inward on inspiration.

frames.text: Flail: ≥2 contiguous ribs, each broken in ≥2 places
Hess: also sternal fracture or costochondral separation
Flail segment: IN on inspiration, OUT on expiration
Serious injury → hypoxia if untreated
Tx: positive pressure → now surgical rib stabilization

q: Per the course notes, flail chest is defined as:
o: Two or more contiguous rib fractures with two or more breaks per rib
A single rib fractured in one place
Two ribs, each fractured in only one place
Any rib fracture with a pneumothorax
e: Flail chest: defined as two or more contiguous rib fractures with two or more breaks per rib.

q: During inspiration, a flail segment:
o: Moves outward with the rest of the thorax
Is pushed outward by positive intrapleural pressure
e: During inspiration, the flail segment is drawn into the chest (negative intrapleural pressure) while the rest of the thorax expands outward.

frames.text: Slides: adult female 7.0–8.0, male 8.0–9.0 mm ID
Hess: women 7–7.5, men 8–8.5 mm ID
Have one size larger AND one size smaller ready
Oral depth: male 21–23 cm, female 19–21 cm

q: Per the course lecture notes, the typical ETT size for an adult male is:
e: Course notes: adult male → 8.0–9.0 mm ID; adult female → 7.0–8.0 mm ID. Hess gives a smaller range (8 to 8.5 mm for men, 7 to 7.5 mm for women); the course uses 8.0–9.0.

q: Besides the expected ETT size, what should you have immediately available?
o: One size larger and one size smaller
e: Choose the expected size → have one size larger AND one size smaller immediately available.

frames.text: Uncuffed ETT ID ≈ (age ÷ 4) + 4
Cuffed ETT ID ≈ (age ÷ 4) + 3.5
Length-based tape: kids 35 kg or less
Uncuffed: premature infants or < 3 kg

q: Using the course formula, the UNCUFFED ETT size for a 4-year-old is:
e: Uncuffed ETT ID ≈ (age ÷ 4) + 4, so 4 ÷ 4 + 4 = 5.0 mm. Cuffed would be 4 ÷ 4 + 3.5 = 4.5 mm.

q: Uncuffed ETTs are recommended for:
o: Premature infants or those weighing less than 3 kg
Only children weighing more than 35 kg
e: Uncuffed tubes are recommended for premature infants or those weighing less than 3 kg; both cuffed and uncuffed tubes are acceptable for infants and children.

q: Per Hess, length-based tapes for estimating ETT size are generally useful for children weighing:
e: Length-based tapes are generally considered useful for children weighing 35 kg or less.

frames.text: Neonates: size by weight (Hess Table 22-8)
Weight unknown? Gestational age predicts size
Neonatal depth from lips ≈ weight (kg) + 6 cm

q: A neonate weighs 1500 g. Per Hess, the suggested ETT size (mm ID) is:
Per Hess, a neonate weighing less than 1000 g needs an ETT of about:
e: Hess Table 22-8: less than 1000 g → 2.5 mm; 1000 to 2000 g → 3.0 mm.

frames.text: OSA: throat muscles relax → airway blocked
CSA: brain doesn't signal the breathing muscles
OSA is more common; CSA is less common

q: Which statement describes CENTRAL sleep apnea?
o: The brain doesn't send proper signals to the breathing muscles
The throat muscles relax and block the airway
The upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep
It is more common than obstructive sleep apnea
e: CSA occurs because the brain doesn't send proper signals to the muscles that control breathing. Relaxed throat muscles and upper-airway collapse describe OSA, and CSA is less common than OSA.

q: Which type of sleep apnea is more common?
e: Central sleep apnea is less common than obstructive sleep apnea; OSA is the most common type.

frames.text: Obstructive: effort, but no airflow
Central: no effort + no airflow
Esophageal pressure: ↑ effort in OSA, absent in CSA
CSA on PSG: no airflow, no thoracoabdominal movement
Mixed: starts central, ends obstructive → treat as OSA

q: A sleep study shows absent airflow with continued respiratory effort. This is:
e: Effort but no airflow = obstructive. No effort + no airflow = central; mixed starts central (no effort) and ends obstructive.

q: A patient whose events are predominantly MIXED apneas is classified and treated as having:
e: Clinically, patients with predominantly mixed apnea are classified and treated as having OSA.

q: On the esophageal pressure tracing, a CENTRAL apnea shows:
o: Effort that starts absent and then appears
e: Central apnea: esophageal pressure is also absent, no effort to breathe. Obstructive shows increased effort; mixed starts flat, then effort appears.

frames.text: CSA causes: Cheyne-Stokes (HF), CNS, drugs, altitude
OSA: genioglossus fails → tongue blocks airway
CSA Tx: start by treating the underlying cause
BiPAP: indicated for sleep apnea, esp. central

q: Which is a common cause of secondary CENTRAL sleep apnea?
o: The genioglossus failing to hold the tongue forward
Throat muscles relaxing and blocking the airway
Recurring collapse of the upper airway
e: Common causes of secondary CSA include Cheyne-Stokes breathing (heart failure). The other choices are OSA mechanisms.

q: During CPAP titration, the patient shows periods of central sleep apnea. You should consider:
e: If the patient exhibits periods of central sleep apnea during titration, consider a trial of BiPAP.

frames.text: Heliox ↓ work of breathing: large airway obstruction, severe asthma
Always ≥ 20% O2 with helium
Hess: FiO2 > 0.40 needed → helium unlikely to help

q: To ensure patient safety, helium should always be combined with at least what O2 concentration?
e: Always use helium combined with at least 20% O2. Pure (100%) helium would cause anoxia.

q: Which is one of the three standard premixed heliox cylinders listed in the slides?
e: Premixed cylinders: 80% He/20% O2, 70% He/30% O2, 60% He/40% O2. Always use at least 20% O2.

q: Why does heliox reduce the work of breathing?
o: Helium is much less dense than nitrogen, so resistance to airflow drops
Helium is denser than nitrogen and splints the airways open
Heliox delivers more O2 than pure oxygen
e: Helium is much less dense than nitrogen, reducing resistance to airflow. Heliox has a lower O2 concentration than pure oxygen therapy.

frames.text: Spontaneous breathing: tight-fitting nonrebreathing mask
Hess: sealed system; mask with reservoir bag, 12–15 L/min
Ventilated pts too: cuffed airway or noninvasive
Always monitor FiO2 with an alarmed O2 analyzer
Heliox-powered nebulizer: ↑ flow 50% to 100%

q: Per the slides, heliox for a spontaneously breathing patient is generally delivered via:
o: A blow-by tube held near the face
Pure helium through a simple cannula
e: Heliox generally is delivered via a tight-fitting nonrebreathing mask. Hess: a tightly sealed closed system is required because helium leaks easily, and pure helium is never used.

q: When heliox is used to power a nebulizer, Hess says the flow should be:
e: When heliox is used to power the nebulizer, the flow should be increased by 50% to 100% to ensure adequate output.

frames.text: O2 flowmeter? Apply a correction factor
10 L/min shown × 1.8 = 18 L/min actual (80% He/20% O2)
Hess agrees: 80% He/20% O2 flow is 1.8× the indicated flow

q: What is the flowmeter correction factor for 70% He / 30% O2?
e: Correction factors: 1.8 for 80/20, 1.6 for 70/30, 1.4 for 60/40.

q: An O2 flowmeter reads 10 L/min while delivering 80% He / 20% O2. What is the actual heliox flow?
e: 10 L/min × 1.8 (factor for 80/20) = 18 L/min.

frames.text: Diagnostic = find disease; Therapeutic = treat
Dx: unknown CXR lesions, hemoptysis source
Dx: unexplained cough, localized wheeze, stridor
Dx: samples for cytology/microbiology (BAL, biopsy)
BAL: key tool for bacterial VAP

q: Which is an indication for a DIAGNOSTIC (not therapeutic) bronchoscopy?
o: Clearing mucus plugs causing lobar atelectasis
Facilitating ETT insertion in a difficult intubation
e: Investigating the source of hemoptysis is a diagnostic indication. Clearing mucus plugs, stent placement, and difficult intubation are therapeutic indications.

q: BAL is a key tool for diagnosing which condition?
e: BAL is a key tool for diagnosing bacterial VAP. OSA is diagnosed by polysomnography, tension pneumothorax clinically, and hyperresponsiveness by methacholine challenge.

frames.text: Tx: clear mucus plugs causing atelectasis
Tx: remove foreign bodies / abnormal tissue
Tx: difficult intubation, selective mainstem intubation
Tx: airway stents, balloon dilation of stenosis
Flexible = routine exam; rigid = airway control, big obstruction

q: Which is an indication for a THERAPEUTIC bronchoscopy?
o: Clearing mucus plugs causing lobar atelectasis
Assessing a lesion of unknown etiology on chest x-ray
Following up on positive sputum cytology
e: Locating and clearing mucus plugs causing lobar or segmental atelectasis is therapeutic. The other choices are diagnostic indications.

q: Which type of bronchoscopy is particularly valuable when airway control or removal of a large obstruction is needed?
e: Flexible bronchoscopy is preferred for routine airway examination; rigid is particularly valuable for airway control or removing a large obstruction.

frames.text: Lidocaine: topical (local) anesthesia
Benzos: sedation/amnesia; opioids: analgesia, ↓ cough
Reversal: naloxone (opioids), flumazenil (benzos)
Propofol: rapid onset, short acting; no reversal agent
Atropine: vent-procedures deck lists it; Hess: many centers dropped it

q: Which drug is used for topical (local) anesthesia of the airway during bronchoscopy?
e: Topical lidocaine provides local anesthesia; midazolam (benzo) sedates, fentanyl (opioid) gives analgesia, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

q: After bronchoscopy with midazolam, the patient is oversedated. Which reversal agent fits?
o: There is no reversal agent for midazolam
e: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines (midazolam); naloxone reverses narcotics. Naloxone does not reverse Midazolam.

q: Which bronchoscopy sedative has NO specific reversal agent?
e: Propofol is neither an opioid nor a benzodiazepine and has no specific reversal agent. Opioids → naloxone; benzodiazepines → flumazenil.

frames.text: Vent-procedures deck: lidocaine 5 to 10 mL of 1% to 4%, aerosol
Hess: total lidocaine ≤ 5 to 7 mg/kg
Same deck: morphine for cough + pain; diazepam sedates
Bleeding: epinephrine or thrombin; iced saline
After: no food/drink until gag reflex returns

q: Per Hess, the total topical lidocaine dose during bronchoscopy should not exceed:
o: There is no dose limit for topical lidocaine
e: The total lidocaine dose should not exceed 5 to 7 mg/kg, adjusted downward with significant hepatic or cardiac disease.

q: Which medications are instilled through the bronchoscope to control bleeding?
e: Therapies to stop bleeding include epinephrine or thrombin (plus non-drug iced saline), given via the working channel.

frames.text: RRT = Medical Emergency Team (MET)
Goal: act in the pre-arrest period
Any staff member may call; often RT + critical care RN

q: The main goal of a rapid response team is to:
o: Intervene in the pre-arrest period to prevent ICU transfer, arrest, or death
Respond only after cardiac arrest has occurred
Care only for patients already in the ICU
Wait until the patient is transferred to the ICU
e: RRTs intervene during the critical pre-arrest period, with the goal of preventing ICU transfer, cardiac arrest, or death. They also proactively evaluate high-risk ward patients.

q: Per Hess, who may call the rapid response team?
e: Any staff member may call the team if a criterion is met; some hospitals even encourage patients or family members to activate it.

frames.text: RR > 28 or < 8
SBP > 180 or < 90 mm Hg
SpO2 < 89% despite supplemental O2
Mental status change; urine < 50 mL over 4 h

q: Which heart rate meets Hess's criteria to call the rapid response team?
o: More than 140 or less than 40 beats/min
More than 100 or less than 60 beats/min
More than 120 or less than 50 beats/min
More than 180 or less than 30 beats/min
e: Activation criterion: heart rate more than 140 beats/min or less than 40 beats/min.

q: Which respiratory rate meets Hess's criteria to call the rapid response team?
o: More than 28 or less than 8 breaths/min
More than 20 or less than 12 breaths/min
More than 35 or less than 5 breaths/min
More than 24 or less than 10 breaths/min
e: Activation criterion: respiratory rate more than 28 breaths/min or less than 8 breaths/min.

q: Which systolic blood pressure meets Hess's criteria to call the rapid response team?
o: More than 180 or less than 90 mm Hg
More than 140 or less than 100 mm Hg
More than 160 or less than 100 mm Hg
More than 200 or less than 70 mm Hg
e: Activation criterion: systolic blood pressure more than 180 mm Hg or less than 90 mm Hg.

q: Which oxygenation finding meets Hess's criteria to call the rapid response team?
o: SpO2 less than 89% despite oxygen supplementation
SpO2 less than 95% on room air
SpO2 of 92% on 2 L/min nasal cannula
e: Activation criterion: oxygen saturation less than 89% despite oxygen supplementation.

frames.text: Also: chest pain unrelieved by NTG, airway patency, seizure, stroke signs
Staff concern alone is enough
Post-op: highest risk in the first 12–24 h
Recent ICU transfer-outs: risk within 24 h
Laryngectomy pt obstructing? Call the RRT

q: Which urine output meets Hess's criteria to call the rapid response team?
e: Activation criterion: urine output less than 50 mL over 4 hours.

q: A nurse is worried about a patient whose vital signs are still within limits. Per Hess, can the RRT be called?
o: Yes, significant staff concern is a criterion
No, a vital sign must be abnormal
No, only a physician can decide
Only if the patient is in cardiac arrest
e: Any staff member may call the team; one criterion is that a staff member has significant concern about the patient's condition.

frames.text: VT: gas in/out with normal breathing; IRV: max extra in
ERV: max out from resting expiration; RV: left after max expiration
Capacities = two or more volumes
VC = VT + IRV + ERV
IC = VT + IRV; FRC = RV + ERV
TLC: gas in lungs at end of maximal inspiration
FRC is the key: RV = FRC − ERV; TLC = FRC + IC
Slide normals: RV 1.2 L, FRC 2.4 L, TLC 6.0 L
Weaning deck: VC ≈ 4.8 L = IRV 3.1 + VT 0.5 + ERV 1.2
Obstructive: air trapping → ↑ RV, ↑ FRC, TLC normal or ↑
Restrictive: small lungs → ↓ RV, ↓ FRC, ↓ TLC
FVC: air rapidly exhaled from TLC (minimum 6 s)
FEV1/FVC separates obstructive from restrictive
Slides: FEV1/FVC < 70% = obstruction; Hess: below LLN
FEF25–75%: flow between 25% and 75% of the FVC
Low FEF25–75% = early small-airway obstruction
Hess: FEF measures add little unique information
↓ FEV1/FVC → obstructive
Normal ratio + ↓ FVC → restriction suspected; TLC confirms
Slides: abnormal = < 80% predicted (VC, TLC, DLCO)
Hess: the 80%-of-predicted rule is invalid; use LLN
DLCO tells why: ↓ in emphysema and ILD
FRC needs special tests: N2 washout, He dilution, body box
N2 washout: breathe 100% O2, open circuit
Body box measures all thoracic gas (TGV), incl. trapped gas
Pitfalls: leak → falsely high FRC; obstruction → underestimate
Reversible: FEV1 or FVC ↑ ≥ 12% AND ≥ 200 mL
% change = (post − pre) ÷ pre × 100
Retest timing: slides 15–30 min; Hess 10–15 min
Bronchoprovocation test = methacholine challenge
Methacholine provokes bronchospasm in hyperresponsive airways
Positive: FEV1 falls ≥ 20% (PD20)
Avoid in moderate–severe obstruction; reverse with albuterol

q: Which is the volume of gas remaining in the lungs after a maximal expiration?
e: RV is the gas remaining after a maximal expiration. ERV is what can be expired from a resting expiration; FRC is the gas left at the end of a resting expiration.

q: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the sum of:
e: FRC = RV + ERV. VT + IRV is the IC; VT + IRV + ERV is the VC; RV + VC is the TLC.

q: Per the course slides, a normal total lung capacity (TLC) is about:
e: Slide values: TLC 6.0 L, FRC 2.4 L, RV 1.2 L.

q: Which static lung volume finding confirms a restrictive defect?
o: Normal FEV1/FVC with a low FVC
e: A decreased TLC confirms restriction. Increased RV and FRC are air trapping (obstruction). A normal ratio with a low FVC only suggests restriction until TLC confirms it.

q: Per the course PFT interpretation slides, an FEV1/FVC (FEV1%) below what value is considered abnormal (obstruction)?
e: Slides: less than normal is < 70% for the FEV1%; the < 80% predicted cutoff is for VC, TLC, and DLCO.

q: According to Hess, an obstructive ventilatory defect is defined as:
o: FEV1/FVC below the lower limit of normal (LLN)
FEV1/FVC below a fixed 0.7 for every patient
e: Hess: an obstructive defect is an FEV1/FVC ratio below the LLN; a fixed 0.7 should not be used, the 80% of predicted rule should be abandoned, and FEF measures add little unique information.

q: Per the slides, an FEF25–75% at 70% of predicted or less indicates:
e: Slides: FEF25–75% ≤ 70% of predicted = small airway obstruction; FEF200–1200 ≤ 70% = large airway obstruction. Restriction is a volume problem judged by FVC.

q: Spirometry shows a normal FEV1/FVC with a decreased FVC. Per the course slides, the next interpretation is:
o: Restriction suspected; confirm with lung volumes (TLC)
Restriction confirmed; no further testing needed
e: Normal FEV1/FVC + ↓ FVC → restrictive suspected; restriction requires lung volumes/TLC for confirmation. A decreased ratio would mean obstruction.

q: PFTs show obstruction with a decreased DLCO. This pattern points to:
e: Obstruction + ↓ DLCO → emphysema; obstruction + normal DLCO → asthma/chronic bronchitis; restriction + ↓ DLCO → ILD; restriction + normal DLCO → chest wall/neuromuscular.

q: Which lung volume test measures all thoracic gas, including trapped gas that does not communicate with the airways?
e: Helium dilution and nitrogen washout measure only communicating gas; body plethysmography measures all gas spaces (TGV). A spirometer cannot measure FRC.

q: A leak during a helium dilution test makes the measured FRC:
e: Hess: any leaks occurring during the procedure will give a falsely high FRC.

q: FEV1 rises from 3.0 L before to 3.3 L after a bronchodilator. Per the slides, this is:
o: A 10% change: not a significant response
Significant, because the gain is ≥ 200 mL
e: (3.3 − 3.0) ÷ 3.0 × 100 = 10%. Significance needs ≥ 12% AND ≥ 200 mL, so 300 mL alone does not qualify.

q: Which result defines a significant (reversible) bronchodilator response?
o: FEV1 or FVC rises ≥ 12% AND ≥ 200 mL
e: ≥ 12% AND ≥ 200 mL in FEV1 or FVC = reversible. A ≥ 20% FEV1 fall is a positive methacholine challenge; FEV1/FVC < 70% is obstruction; a ≥ 15% supine SVC fall suggests muscle weakness.

q: A methacholine challenge is positive for airway hyperresponsiveness when the FEV1:
e: ≥ 20% decrease in FEV1 indicates hyperresponsiveness (PD20). If FEV1 stays above 80% of baseline (less than a 20% fall), the dose is increased instead.

q: Bronchial challenge (methacholine) testing is contraindicated in a patient with:
e: Challenge tests are contraindicated with moderate to severe obstruction but very safe with normal baseline spirometry; they are used when spirometry is nondiagnostic and appear in chronic cough workups.

frames.text: Transtracheal catheter: O2 straight into the trachea through the neck
Used to conserve O2: lower flow, upper-airway dead space bypassed
Low-flow device; hidden from view → better adherence
Not the same: transtracheal aspiration = needle sputum sample, no longer used
OPA keeps the tongue off the posterior pharynx
OPA: unconscious, NO gag reflex
Size: corner of mouth → angle of jaw; also a suction path / bite block
NPA: conscious or unconscious; gag reflex may be present
Size: nares → earlobe; lubricate, follow the floor, never force
Use for frequent NT suctioning; avoid in basilar skull / midface fracture
LMA: cuffed mask sits above the glottis (supraglottic)
Used for emergency/difficult airways and general anesthesia
Limits: short-term; less aspiration protection than a cuffed ETT
Trach: bypass upper-airway obstruction, clear secretions, long-term vent
Vs ETT: lower resistance, less movement, more comfort, can swallow
Obturator: insert, remove at once, keep at bedside; spare inner cannula
Trach button: keeps the stoma open
Plugged button → breathe and cough via upper airway
No cuff: limited value with aspiration risk or PPV

q: Which statement about a transtracheal O2 catheter is correct?
o: O2 is usually delivered at a lower flow because upper-airway dead space is bypassed
It is a high-flow device that delivers a fixed FiO2
It is placed through the nose into the nasopharynx
It needs higher flows than a nasal cannula
e: The catheter enters the trachea through the front of the neck; O2 flow is lower because upper-airway dead space is bypassed. Hess lists it among low-flow devices.

q: An oropharyngeal airway (OPA) is appropriate for a patient who is:
o: Unconscious, without an intact gag reflex
Semi-conscious, with an intact gag reflex
Any patient, whether or not the gag reflex is intact
e: OPA: unconscious, no gag reflex. Do not use an OPA in a conscious/semi-conscious patient with a gag reflex; consider an NPA instead.

q: How do you size a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA)?
o: Corner of mouth to angle of jaw
e: NPA: nares to earlobe. Corner of mouth to angle of jaw sizes an OPA. Sizing is based on anatomy, not age alone.

q: Which is a major contraindication to inserting an NPA?
o: Suspected basilar skull fracture or significant midface trauma
e: Avoid an NPA with suspected basilar skull fracture or midface trauma. NPAs can be used with a gag reflex, in conscious or unconscious patients, and to reduce trauma from frequent suctioning.

q: A correctly placed laryngeal mask airway (LMA) sits:
o: Above the glottis, sealing around the laryngeal inlet
Through the vocal cords, inside the trachea
With its tip in the esophagus, like a King LT
In the mouth only, holding the tongue forward like an OPA
e: The LMA is supraglottic: it sits above the glottis and does not enter the trachea or the esophagus. The King LT is the device whose tip enters the esophagus.

q: Compared with a cuffed endotracheal tube, an LMA:
o: Must pass through the vocal cords
e: The LMA provides ventilation but less aspiration protection than a cuffed ETT and is generally used for short periods.

q: Which is a main reason for performing a tracheostomy?
o: To keep the tongue off the posterior pharynx in an unconscious patient
To conserve oxygen by bypassing upper-airway dead space
To keep an existing stoma open without a full tube
e: Hess: tracheostomy bypasses upper airway obstruction, aids secretion removal, and provides long-term ventilation. The other choices describe an OPA, a transtracheal O2 catheter, and a trach button.

q: A tracheostomy button is mainly used to:
o: Maintain the stoma for later trach replacement or suctioning
Provide a cuffed, sealed airway for positive pressure ventilation
Protect a patient at high risk of aspiration
Keep the tongue off the posterior pharynx
e: Buttons maintain the stoma. They have no cuff, so they have limited value with aspiration risk or positive pressure ventilation (leakage occurs).

q: When a tracheostomy button is plugged, the patient:
o: Breathes and coughs through the upper airway
Can no longer breathe and must be ventilated
e: A plug seals the button, forcing the patient to breathe and cough via the upper airway (nose/mouth).

frames.text: PDPV loosens and clears secretions
Manual vs mechanical: equally effective; choose by preference
Vibration: rapid shaking of the chest wall during expiration
Hess: use if > 30 mL/day sputum; slides: stop at < 30 mL/day + effective cough
Hess: little added benefit; avoid over burns, wounds, new pacemaker
IPPB: short-term mechanical ventilation for hyperinflation
When: atelectasis, weak cough, neuromuscular, kyphoscoliosis
How: breaths ≥ 25% above VT, I:E ≈ 1:3, ≤ 20 min
Last resort: only after other lung-expansion options fail
Vibratory PEP = PEP + airway oscillations
Flutter: steel ball, gravity-dependent; Acapella: lever + magnet
When: to mobilize retained secretions
How: upright, PEP 10–20 cm H2O, sets of 10–20 breaths, ≤ 20 min
Avoid: can't tolerate ↑ WOB, unstable, untreated pneumothorax

q: Per the course slides, compared with manual clapping, mechanical percussors:
o: Deliver a consistent rate and force without user fatigue
Should be used only when manual percussion fails
Can be used only in mechanically ventilated patients
e: Mechanical percussors are equally effective, deliver consistent rates and force, and do not fatigue the user; choose by patient preference, convenience, and availability.

q: Per the course slides, PDPV should be discontinued when:
o: Sputum drops below 30 mL/day and the patient has an effective spontaneous cough
The cough is effective, whatever the sputum volume
Sputum drops below 50 mL/day, whatever the cough
e: Both conditions are needed: sputum < 30 mL/day AND an effective spontaneous cough. Hess reserves drainage for patients producing more than 30 mL/day.

q: Which best describes IPPB?
o: Short-term or episodic mechanical ventilation to assist ventilation and give brief hyperinflation
Exhaling through a resistor to create positive expiratory pressure
An inflatable vest that delivers rapid positive-pressure bursts to the chest
Rapid clapping of the chest wall with cupped hands
e: IPPB is episodic mechanical ventilation for ventilation assistance and short-duration hyperinflation. PEP uses an expiratory resistor; HFCWO uses an inflatable vest; clapping with cupped hands is percussion.

q: During IPPB for lung expansion, the delivered breaths should be:
o: At least 25% larger than the patient's tidal volume
Equal to the patient's tidal volume
Smaller than the patient's tidal volume
At least 25% smaller than the patient's tidal volume
e: Hess: adjust the tidal volume during IPPB to deliver breaths at least 25% larger than the patient's tidal volume; the machine inflates the lungs to a larger than normal volume.

q: Per Hess, when should IPPB be used for lung expansion?
o: Only after other alternatives have been exhausted
As first-line therapy for every postoperative patient
Routinely for aerosol delivery, because it outperforms nebulizers
Never; it is contraindicated for lung expansion
e: Hess: consider IPPB for lung expansion only after other alternatives are exhausted; it has no advantage over nebulizers or inhalers for aerosols.

q: Which PEP device works by gravity, so its pressure changes with the device angle?
e: The Flutter depends on gravity (PEP rises when raised above horizontal); the Acapella (lever and magnet), Quake (rotating handle), and other devices such as the Aerobika work independently of gravity.

q: Per the course slides, what PEP level should be targeted during PEP therapy?
e: Start at the lowest level, then slowly increase PEP to between 10 and 20 cm H2O per the manufacturer.

q: PEP therapy should NOT be used in a patient with:
e: Untreated pneumothorax is on the avoid list. PEP is used to prevent or treat atelectasis, reduce air trapping in asthma and COPD, and mobilize secretions.

frames.text: CVP catheter: tip in the SVC near (or in) the right atrium
Used for: fluid status, right-heart function, meds, blood samples
Low CVP guides fluid replacement; inserted via subclavian/jugular
↑ CVP: volume overload, RV failure, pulm HTN, PPV/PEEP; ↓ CVP: hypovolemia
course slides: CVP/RAP 2–6 mm Hg
Hess: CVP 0–8; right atrial pressure 0–7 mm Hg
Chang hemo deck: CVP 0–6 (vena cava), 2–7 mm Hg (right atrium)
PEEP/PPV raises measured CVP; measure at end-expiration
PA (Swan-Ganz) catheter: flow-directed, balloon-tipped
Path: vein → RA → RV → pulmonary artery → wedges in a branch
Today: left heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, cardiac output
PAP, course slides: 15–30 / 8–15 (mean 9–18); Hess: 15–30 / 4–12 (mean 9–16)
Chang hemo deck: normal PAP 15−25/6−12 mm Hg
PCWP (PAWP) estimates left-sided filling pressure
Normal: course slides 6–12 mm Hg; Hess 2–12 mm Hg
Chang hemo deck: 6–12 (some sources 4–12); its wedge slide says 8–12
Balloon up briefly for PCWP; balloon down for PAP
↑ PCWP = left heart problem; cardiogenic edema ↑, ARDS not ↑
Cardiac output: slides 4–8 L/min; Hess list 5–8 (CO = HR × SV)
Cardiac index = CO ÷ BSA; course slides 2.5–4.0 L/min/m²
Hess and Chang hemo deck: CI 2.5–3.5 L/min/m²
Example: CO 4, BSA 2.0 → CI 2.0 = LOW
Diuretics remove excess fluid; water follows salt
Role for RTs: hypertension and CHF; PCWP helps tailor diuretics
Loop (furosemide/Lasix): most potent; CHF and pulmonary edema
IV loop: vasodilation within 5 min → ↓ PCWP, BP, SVR
Thiazide: distal tubule; first line for mild hypertension
K-sparing (spironolactone): blocks aldosterone → hyperkalemia risk
Mannitol: cerebral edema/TBI; acetazolamide: weak, metabolic alkalosis
Side effects: hypovolemia, ↓ K⁺, metabolic alkalosis, loop ototoxicity
Most common combination: loop + thiazide

q: Per the course slides, normal CVP (right atrial pressure) is:
e: Slides: CVP/RAP 2–6 mm Hg; PAWP 6–12; PAP 15–30 / 8–15. (Hess lists CVP 0–8.)

q: Per the course slides, normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is:
e: Slides: PAWP/PCWP 6–12 mm Hg (Hess: 2–12). 2–6 is the slide CVP; 15–30 is PA systolic; above 18 was historically used for cardiogenic edema.

q: CVP reflects the filling pressure of the:
e: CVP is the filling pressure in the right atrium. Left atrial (left-sided) filling pressure is estimated by PAWP.

q: Which measurement is made with the pulmonary artery catheter balloon deflated?
o: Neither; both need the balloon inflated
Both; the balloon is never inflated
e: PAP is measured with the balloon deflated; PCWP is obtained with the balloon inflated momentarily.

q: A patient with pulmonary edema has an elevated PCWP. This most likely indicates:
e: ↑ PAWP → left heart problem; cardiogenic edema tends to elevate PAWP, while ARDS generally does not. Hypovolemia lowers PAWP; distributive shock can have a low or normal wedge.

q: Per the course slides, normal cardiac output and cardiac index are:
e: Slides: CO 4–8 L/min; CI 2.5–4.0 L/min/m² (Hess gives CI 2.5–3.5).

q: Cardiac output is 4 L/min and body surface area is 2.0 m². The cardiac index is:
e: CI = CO ÷ BSA = 4 ÷ 2 = 2.0 L/min/m², below the 2.5–4.0 normal range, so low.

q: IV furosemide (Lasix) given for acute pulmonary edema, within minutes and before diuresis, causes:
o: Vasodilation that lowers PCWP, BP, and SVR
Vasoconstriction that raises BP and SVR
e: IV loops cause acute vasodilation within five minutes, decreasing PCWP, BP, and SVR. Loops cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.

q: Which diuretic is the go-to drug for CHF with pulmonary edema?
e: Loop diuretics (furosemide) are first-line for pulmonary edema/CHF. Mannitol is for cerebral edema/TBI, acetazolamide is a very weak diuretic, and thiazides are first-line for mild HTN, not acute pulmonary edema.

q: Which diuretic class can cause life-threatening hyperkalemia?
e: Potassium-sparing diuretics may cause hyperkalemia, more life-threatening than K+ depletion. Loops and thiazides cause hypokalemia, and hypokalemia is a common adverse effect of CAIs.

q: Diuretic-induced hypokalemia plus hypochloremia most often produces:
e: Hypokalemia + hypochloremia may cause metabolic alkalosis. Metabolic acidosis is the CAI (acetazolamide) exception.

frames.text: C(a-v)O2 = arterial O2 content − mixed venous O2 content
Mixed venous sample: pulmonary artery; SvO2 75%, PvO2 40 mm Hg
Hess normal-values table (venous): SO2 65–75%, PO2 35–45 mm Hg
Normal CaO2: slides 16–22 mL O2/dL; Hess example ≈ 20
Normal C(a-v)O2: 5 mL/dL (Hess normal-values table)
At rest, tissues extract about 25% of delivered O2
↑ extraction (exercise, CHF, anemia) → lower CvO2; sepsis → higher

q: How is the C(a-v)O2 calculated?
o: Arterial O2 content minus mixed venous O2 content
Arterial O2 content times cardiac output
Mixed venous saturation minus arterial saturation
Cardiac output divided by body surface area
e: C(a-v)O2 is the difference between arterial and venous O2 content (CaO2 − CvO2). CaO2 × cardiac output gives O2 delivery (DO2).

q: Using Hess's normal resting values (CaO2 20 mL/100 mL, mixed venous O2 content 15 mL/100 mL), the C(a-v)O2 is:
e: C(a-v)O2 = CaO2 − CvO2 = 20 − 15 = 5 mL/dL, the normal C(a-v)O2 in Hess's normal-values table. 15 and 20 are the venous and arterial contents themselves.

q: Per Hess, normal mixed venous O2 saturation and PO2 are:
e: Mixed venous SO2 and PO2 are normally 75% and 40 mm Hg. 97% and 100 mm Hg are arterial values in Hess's CaO2 example.

q: At rest, tissues normally extract about what fraction of the O2 delivered to them?
e: Resting extraction is about 25%; it can rise to more than 50% to 60% only at maximal exercise.

q: Hess's normal-values table lists a normal C(a-v)O2 of:
e: Hess: C(a-v)O2 5 mL/dL. About 15 and 20 mL/100 mL are Hess's resting mixed venous and arterial contents; 16–22 mL/dL is the slides' normal CaO2.

frames.text: Low-flow (variable FiO2): partial rebreather, nonrebreather
High-flow (fixed FiO2): Venturi mask, air-entrainment nebulizer
High-flow = enough premixed gas that no room air is inhaled
Partial rebreather: simple mask + NONvalved 300–600 mL bag
8–15 L/min, keep bag partly inflated → FiO2 0.4–0.7
For severe hypoxemia; rarely used today
NRB = partial rebreather + one-way VALVES
Exhaled gas never enters the bag
10–15 L/min → FiO2 0.6–0.8; Hess device table 60–80%; recap 0.60–0.90
Bag never > half empty; for trauma, MI, CO exposure
Suffocation risk if valves stick or O2 fails
Aerosol mask: on a large-volume nebulizer via 22-mm tubing
Used for cool, humidified O2 (e.g., after extubation, stridor)
FiO2 set by collar ~0.3–1.0; truly high-flow only at ≤ 0.4
Mist vanishes on inspiration = air dilution → add flow
Air-entrainment (Venturi) mask: jet nozzle + entrainment ports
Bigger ports/smaller jet → more air, ↓ FiO2, ↑ total flow
Turning up O2 L/min changes total flow, not FiO2
For: hypoxemia not controlled on a cannula; hypoventilators
Hess AE mask table: FiO2 0.24–0.70; limited flow above FiO2 0.4

q: What converts a nonrebreathing mask into a partial rebreathing mask?
o: Attaching it to a large-volume nebulizer
e: Removing the valves converts an NRB to a partial rebreather; the partial rebreather still has a (nonvalved) reservoir bag. Large-volume nebulizers drive aerosol masks.

q: Per Hess, a partial rebreathing mask delivers an FiO2 of about:
e: Partial rebreather: 0.40–0.70. The NRB reaches 0.60–0.90; a low-flow nasal cannula gives 0.24–0.40.

q: Which of these delivers a fixed FiO2 (high-flow device)?
e: The Venturi mask is high-flow (fixed FiO2). Partial and non-rebreather masks are low-flow (variable FiO2).

q: On an air-entrainment (Venturi) mask, turning up the O2 flowmeter will:
e: Changing O2 input does not alter the air/O2 ratio or delivered O2%, only the total output flow.

q: Bed sheets block the entrainment ports of a Venturi mask. The delivered FiO2 will:
e: Obstructing the ports decreases air entrainment: higher FiO2 but lower overall flow.

q: During inspiration the mist disappears from a patient's aerosol mask. This means:
o: Room air is diluting the gas (now low-flow); add flow
The FiO2 is higher than set
The system is working as a fixed-FiO2 device
Total flow is higher than the patient needs
e: Mist disappearing indicates air dilution; the high-flow system becomes low-flow with a variable FiO2, so more flow may be needed.

q: On a nonrebreathing mask, set the O2 flow so that the reservoir bag:
o: Never empties by more than half
e: The O2 flow must be high enough to prevent the bag from emptying by more than half.

q: Which patient is the best fit for a nonrebreathing mask?
o: Carbon monoxide exposure, needs a high FiO2, fairly normal breathing pattern
Hypoventilating patient who needs a moderate, controlled FiO2
Patient needing cool bland mist after extubation
Patient who needs a precise low FiO2 such as 0.28
e: NRB: high FiO2 with a relatively normal pattern (trauma, MI, CO exposure). Hypoventilators on a moderate FiO2 and precise low-FiO2 needs suit an air-entrainment mask; cool mist uses an aerosol mask.

q: Which device does Hess say delivers a precise flow at a low FiO2 but has limited ability to provide flow above an FiO2 of 0.4?
e: Hess's recap: air-entrainment masks deliver a precise flow when a low FiO2 is specified but have limited ability to provide flows above 0.4. The others are low-flow, variable-FiO2 devices.

frames.text: Shunt = perfusion WITHOUT ventilation
V/Q mismatch = both present, but not matched
Hess V/Q ratio: normal 0.8 · shunt 0 · dead space ∞
Shunt causes: atelectasis, PNA, ARDS, pulmonary edema
V/Q mismatch causes: COPD, asthma, PNA, edema, PE

q: "Perfusion without ventilation" describes which mechanism?
e: Shunt = perfusion without ventilation; blood passes through the lungs but never sees oxygen. Dead space is ventilation without perfusion.

q: Per Hess, what is the V/Q ratio of a shunt?
e: Hess Respiratory Recap: ideal V/Q 1.0, normal 0.8, shunt 0, dead space infinity.

q: What is the most common cause of hypoxemia?
e: V/Q mismatch is the most common cause of hypoxemia (a huge NBRC favorite).

frames.text: V/Q mismatch improves with O2; shunt often does not
Shunt → refractory hypoxemia
Significant shunt: P/F < 200, or PaO2 ≤ 50 on FiO2 ≥ 50%
Treat shunt: CPAP/PEEP (recruitment), proning
A-a gradient: 66–300 = V/Q mismatch; >300 = shunt

q: Which mechanism of hypoxemia is LEAST responsive to oxygen therapy?
e: Shunt: blood passes alveoli that receive no ventilation, so more O2 can't reach it. Hess: O2 increases PaO2 best in hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, and diffusion defect; it is least effective when right-to-left shunt predominates.

q: Per the course notes, an A-a gradient greater than 300 mmHg points to:
e: Course notes: A-a gradient 5–15 mmHg on RA is normal; 66–300 mmHg = V/Q mismatch (O2 up to 60%); >300 mmHg = shunting (vent with PEEP).

q: Per the course slides, significant shunting generally exists when:
o: P/F ratio drops below 200, or oxygenation can't be maintained on 50% or more O2
Hypoxemia responds well to supplemental oxygen alone
The A-a gradient is 5–15 mmHg on room air
e: Significant shunting generally exists when the P/F ratio drops below 200 or you cannot maintain satisfactory arterial oxygenation on 50% or more oxygen (PaO2 ≤ 50 torr on FiO2 ≥ 50%). Then O2 alone is insufficient; treatment is normally CPAP or PEEP.

frames.text: Normal physiologic shunt: about 2–5% of cardiac output
Proning reduces shunt and improves V/Q matching
PE: lost perfusion → high V/Q (alveolar dead space)

q: Which condition do the course notes call the "classic severe shunt condition"?
e: ARDS is the classic severe shunt condition: many alveoli are collapsed and fluid-filled, perfusion persists, ventilation is absent. PE reduces perfusion (high V/Q), fibrosis is a diffusion defect, and drug overdose causes hypoventilation.

q: Per the course slides, reduced perfusion to ventilated alveoli (e.g., pulmonary embolism) produces:
e: High V/Q mismatch comes from reduced pulmonary perfusion (e.g., PE): plenty of air, not enough blood. Low V/Q comes from reduced ventilation (e.g., airflow obstruction); shunt is perfusion without ventilation. Hess adds that the hypoxemia of PE comes from low-V/Q regions and shunting through atelectatic areas, but the perfusion loss itself is high V/Q.

frames.text: VC: volume guaranteed, pressure varies · PC: pressure guaranteed, volume varies
Independent variable = what the vent guarantees (VC: volume; PC: pressure)
Stiffer lungs: VC → same VT, higher pressure · PC → same pressure, lower VT
Chang slides: VC 1st choice, PC 2nd · NBRC: either OK; Pplat > 30 in VC → PC

q: A patient on pressure control develops stiffer lungs (lower compliance). What happens?
o: Delivered VT decreases; pressure stays the same
Pressure rises; VT stays the same
e: In PC the pressure is guaranteed, so with stiffer lungs the ventilator still delivers the same pressure but the VT decreases. Rising pressure with constant VT is what happens in VC.

q: During volume-control ventilation, the independent (control) variable is:
e: Whatever the ventilator guarantees is the independent variable. In VC it is volume; pressure is the dependent variable. The control variables are volume, pressure, and time.

frames.text: CMV (Chang slides): preset VT, time-triggered, no patient triggering
CMV needs adequate sedation; NMB may be needed
CMV used for: tetanus/seizures, complete rest, crushed chest, paradoxical chest
CMV risks: prolonged sedation, apnea/hypoxia, respiratory muscle atrophy
Naming conflict: Hess calls continuous mandatory ventilation (CMV) = Assist/Control
A/C: assist = patient-triggered; control = time-triggered
A/C: every breath gets the full preset breath
A/C use: full support, minimize atelectasis · risk: high RR → hyperventilation

q: In the Chang course slides, how does CMV (control mode) differ from A/C?
o: CMV does not allow patient-triggered breaths; A/C does
CMV allows spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths; A/C does not
CMV lets the patient set the VT; A/C does not
CMV has no set rate; A/C does
e: Chang slides: A/C allows patient-triggered breaths; CMV does not (time-triggered, patient trigger and spontaneous breathing not possible). Note Hess uses CMV to mean assist/control.

q: Which is a listed indication for CMV (control mode)?
o: Helping prevent intubation in end-stage COPD
e: CMV indications: tetanus or seizures, complete rest, crushed chest injury, paradoxical chest wall movement. Weaning is an SIMV indication, post-anesthesia recovery is Volume Support, and preventing intubation in COPD is BiPAP.

q: A/C rate is set at 12 and the patient triggers 24 breaths/min. How many fully supported breaths does the patient receive?
e: Every A/C breath, patient- or time-triggered, receives the full preset breath, so all 24 breaths are supported. A split of mandatory plus spontaneous breaths is SIMV behavior.

frames.text: IMV: set mandatory breaths at fixed intervals + spontaneous breaths between
IMV risk: breath stacking / air trapping
Why IMV: keep respiratory muscles working, begin weaning
SIMV = IMV synchronized to patient effort → less breath stacking
Between mandatory breaths: spontaneous breaths at any VT the patient wants
SIMV use: partial support, keep muscle strength, help weaning
SIMV risk: fatigue/weaning failure without PS → add PS

q: What problem of IMV does SIMV reduce?
o: Breath stacking, by synchronizing mandatory breaths with patient effort
Hypoxemia, by delivering tiny VTs at high frequency
High respiratory rates, by giving every breath full support
Barotrauma, by eliminating the set rate
e: IMV risks air trapping or breath stacking when a mechanical breath arrives before a spontaneous breath is exhaled. SIMV synchronizes mandatory breaths with spontaneous effort, so breath stacking is reduced or avoided.

q: Per the course slide, the SIMV rate is 10/min and the patient breathes 20 times/min. The result is:
o: 10 mandatory breaths; extra efforts are ignored
20 spontaneous breaths and no mandatory breaths
e: With IMV/SIMV, extra breaths remain spontaneous: set rate 10, patient triggers 20, result 10 mandatory and 10 spontaneous. In A/C (CMV) the same scenario gives 20 mandatory breaths.

frames.text: MMV: guarantees a preset MINIMUM minute ventilation (SIMV-related)
Spontaneous VE falls below minimum → vent raises mandatory rate
MMV = safety net: breathe enough → vent stays out of the way

q: In MMV, the patient's spontaneous minute ventilation falls below the preset minimum. The ventilator:
o: Increases the pressure support level to keep a target VT
Switches from PRVC to Volume Support
e: MMV automatically increases the mandatory breath frequency when spontaneous minute ventilation falls below the preset minimum. Raising PS for a target VT is Volume Support; PRVC/VS switching is Automode; Phigh to Plow releases are APRV.

frames.text: PSV: patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled
Only on spontaneous breaths; VT set by the patient
Purpose: lower spontaneous WOB; help difficult weaning
PSV indications: low spont VT, high spont rate, ↑WOB · target RR < 25

q: A pressure support breath ends (cycles) when:
o: Inspiratory flow falls to a preset level
Airway pressure reaches the set PS level
e: PSV is flow-cycled: not by volume, not by time, not by pressure. It ends when inspiratory flow drops to a predetermined level.

frames.text: PRVC: volume-targeted breaths at the lowest possible PIP
Adjusts peak flow and I-time as compliance/resistance change
Same idea, other names: Servo PRVC · Dräger AutoFlow · PB840 VC+
Automode: no effort → PRVC; two pt-triggered breaths → Volume Support

q: The goal of PRVC is to:
o: Deliver the target VT at the lowest possible PIP
Guarantee a set pressure and let VT vary
Give support proportional to effort with no volume or pressure target
Deliver very small VTs at very high frequencies
e: PRVC provides volume-controlled breaths while keeping PIP at the lowest level possible. Guaranteed pressure with variable VT is PCV; no target is PAV; tiny VT at high frequency is HFOV.

frames.text: VV+ (Puritan Bennett 840) = VC+ and Volume Support
VC+: mandatory breaths (A/C, SIMV); set VT & I-time; pressure varies
VC+ vents cough/breathing pressure via active exhalation valve → synchrony
Volume Support: target VT; less effort → more PS, more effort → less PS
Volume Support: rate, VE and I-time set by the patient

q: In Volume Support, the patient tires and effort decreases. The ventilator:
o: Raises pressure support to keep the target VT
Raises the mandatory breath rate to a preset minimum VE
Keeps PS fixed and lets VT fall
e: Volume Support guarantees volume: less patient effort brings higher pressure support. Raising the mandatory rate is MMV; fixed PS with falling VT is plain PSV.

frames.text: PCV: time-triggered, pressure-limited, time-cycled
Preset pressure, variable volume (changes with compliance/resistance)
Indication: severe ARDS (stiff lungs) — limit airway pressure
Pressure waveform: VC climbs (mountain) · PC rises fast, stays flat (table)

q: Which mode do the course slides indicate for severe ARDS, when limiting airway pressure matters more than guaranteeing VT?
e: PCV guarantees pressure, not volume, making it useful in severe ARDS. Volume Support is often used in post-anesthesia recovery; CMV is for tetanus, seizures, crushed chest; BiPAP helps prevent intubation in COPD.

frames.text: PAV: no target flow, volume, or pressure
Support ∝ elastance, resistance, and ventilatory demand
Benefit: more uniform breathing · Risk: PS overshoot if mechanics change

q: Which mode has no target flow, volume, or pressure and gives support proportional to patient effort?
e: With PAV there is no target flow, volume, or pressure; support changes with patient effort. PRVC and Volume Support target a VT; PCV targets a pressure.

frames.text: APRV: inverse-ratio, pressure-controlled IMV with unrestricted spontaneous breathing
Most time at Phigh (keeps alveoli open); brief release to Plow (< 1.5 s) removes CO2
No VT setting: VT = Phigh–Plow gradient, varies with compliance & resistance
Use: ARDS / lung protection, in a patient who still has a respiratory drive
Slides differ: APRV 'allows, not requires' vs 'use only if pt can trigger enough'

q: In APRV, delivered VT is determined by:
o: The pressure gradient between Phigh and Plow
e: APRV has no VT setting; VT comes from the Phigh–Plow pressure gradient and varies with compliance and resistance. Amplitude sets VT in HFOV.

frames.text: HFV: 150–900 breaths/min, VT as small as 1–2 mL/kg
Use: hypoxemia not helped by usual methods (ARDS, infant RDS) · Hess: not routine in ARDS
HFOV actively pushes gas IN and actively pulls gas OUT
↑CO2 removal: ↑amplitude or ↓Hz · ↑O2: ↑mean airway pressure or FiO2
Relative contraindications: hypotension, air trapping

q: A patient on HFOV needs more CO2 removal. Which change does that?
e: On HFOV, ventilation increases by decreasing oscillation frequency or increasing amplitude. Mean airway pressure and FiO2 control oxygenation.

frames.text: PEEP raises baseline pressure: keeps alveoli open, ↑FRC, ↑oxygenation
Indications: shunt/refractory hypoxemia, ↓FRC & compliance, stubborn auto-PEEP
Danger: PEEP > 10 (or Paw > 30, PIP > 50 cm H2O) → ↑ barotrauma
Also: ↓venous return → ↓CO → ↓BP; ↑ICP
Optimal PEEP: SpO2 ≥ 88–90% WITHOUT dropping BP

q: PEEP > 10 cm H2O, Paw > 30 cm H2O, or PIP > 50 cm H2O is associated with:
e: The course slide links PEEP > 10, Paw > 30, or PIP > 50 cm H2O to increased alveolar rupture or barotrauma. Higher PEEP decreases venous return and cardiac output and can increase ICP.

frames.text: Trigger = what STARTS the breath · Cycle = what ENDS it
Spontaneous = patient triggers AND cycles; vent controls either → mandatory
Patient-triggered ≠ spontaneous (an A/C breath is still mandatory)
Breath sequences: CMV all mandatory · IMV mixed · CSV all spontaneous
Trigger sensitivity: closer to zero = more sensitive

q: On VC assist/control, the patient triggers a breath and the ventilator ends it after the set volume. This breath is:
o: Mandatory, because the ventilator cycles it
Spontaneous, because the patient triggered it
Spontaneous, because A/C is a CSV sequence
Mandatory, because the ventilator triggered it
e: A breath is spontaneous only if the patient controls both trigger and cycle; if the ventilator controls either, it is mandatory. Patient-triggered is not the same as spontaneous. In the breath-sequence classification (principles deck, Hess), A/C belongs to CMV, not CSV.

frames.text: Asynchrony: vent support doesn't match the patient's ventilatory needs
Course: 3 major categories (trigger & flow figures) · Hess: trigger, cycle, mode
Trigger: auto-cycling from leaks, condensate, or a too-sensitive trigger
Trigger: insensitive setting or auto-PEEP makes the patient work to trigger
Flow: unmet flow demand → scalloped pressure waveform

q: Auto-cycling (extra ventilator breaths without patient effort) is usually caused by:
e: Auto-cycling breaths occur without patient effort, usually from circuit condensate or leaks (or an overly sensitive trigger). Inadequate flow causes scalloping (flow asynchrony); an insensitive trigger makes the patient work harder to trigger.

frames.text: High pressure / ↑Raw: bronchospasm, secretions, edema, kinked or bitten tube
PIP ↑ + Pplat ↑ = compliance problem (e.g., edema, fibrosis, pneumothorax)
Circuit obstruction → high-pressure + low-volume alarms
Low pressure / low volume: disconnection or leak
Set high PIP alarm 10 above PIP (35 initially); low PIP 10 below

q: A ventilator circuit obstruction is associated with which alarms?
e: Circuit obstructions are always associated with low-volume and high-pressure alarms. Leaks and disconnections cause loss of volume and pressure (low-pressure/low-volume alarms).

frames.text: Double-limb circuit: ICU ventilators
Single-limb WITH exhalation valve: home care / transport ventilators
Single-limb WITHOUT valve (leak port): noninvasive ventilators
Most dangerous: blocked exhalation port on a single-limb NPPV circuit

q: A double-limb ventilator circuit is typically used on:
