e: Double-limb circuits are typically used on ICU ventilators. Single-limb circuits with an exhalation valve are used on home care or transport ventilators; single-limb circuits without a valve (port) on noninvasive ventilators.

frames.text: Static compliance (Cstat/Crs) = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP)
Dynamic compliance (Cdyn) = VT ÷ (PIP − PEEP)
Cdyn is always < Crs; the gap reflects airway resistance
Course slides: intubated adult Crs 40–80 mL/cm H2O; < 25–30 = trouble
Other sources: Hess 50–100 on vent (normal 100); principles deck 60–100

q: Per the course slides, normal static compliance (Crs) for an intubated adult is:
e: Course slides: normal Crs for intubated adults is 40–80 mL/cm H2O; below 25–30 is linked to increased WOB. 200 is Hess's lung (not respiratory-system) compliance, and 5–12 is normal Raw in cm H2O/L/sec.

q: In the course PEEP-study example, VT is 600 mL, Pplat 27 cm H2O, and PEEP 10 cm H2O. Static compliance is:
e: Cst = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP): 27 − 10 = 17, and 600/17 = 35.3 mL/cm H2O. 17 is only the pressure difference.

q: Which is true of dynamic compliance (Cdyn)?
o: It uses PIP − PEEP and is always lower than static compliance
It uses Pplat − PEEP and is always higher than static compliance
It is measured only during an end-expiratory hold
It reflects lung elasticity only, not airway resistance
e: Cdyn uses PIP − PEEP, reflects both Crs and Raw, and is always < Crs. Pplat is used for static compliance; an end-expiratory hold measures auto-PEEP. Note: the course Cdyn slide calls PIP − PEEP the driving pressure, while other course notes and Hess define driving pressure as Pplat − PEEP.

frames.text: Minute ventilation = VT × rate (500 mL × 12 = 6 L/min)
VT = alveolar volume + dead space (500 = 350 + 150 mL)
Alveolar ventilation = gas reaching the alveoli (gas-exchanging part)
Only alveolar ventilation affects arterial blood gases
Smaller VT → larger VD/VT (30% at 500 mL → 50% at 300 mL)

q: Which portion of minute ventilation affects arterial blood gases?
o: All of the minute ventilation equally
e: Alveolar ventilation is the only portion of minute ventilation that affects arterial blood gases. Dead space gas moves in and out without taking part in gas exchange.

frames.text: Inspired gas is fully saturated at 37 °C (44 mg/L) below the carina (ISB)
Rain out: heated humidified gas cools → holds less water → condenses
Example: humidifier at 50 °C (>80 mg/L) → 35 °C holds only 40 mg/L
Condensate is contaminated: drain away from the patient, use water traps
Reduce rain out: heated wires, insulated/thick tubing, coaxial circuit

q: Rain out in a heated ventilator circuit happens because:
o: Heated, humidified gas cools and can hold less water
Gas warms in the tubing and holds more water
Heated-wire circuits add extra water to the gas
A coaxial circuit traps humidity in the inspiratory limb
e: As heated, humidified gas cools, its water content declines and condensation (rain out) occurs. Heated wires and coaxial circuits are techniques that reduce condensate.

frames.text: ETT cuff pressure: 20–30 cm H2O
Too high (> 25–30): ischemia → ulceration, necrosis · NBRC high limit 25
Too low: leakage aspiration → VAP
Check every shift; always adjust (not just measure) · course: minimal leak no longer used
Need > 30 to seal? check tube size/position, cuff, trachea

q: The recommended ETT cuff pressure for an adult on positive pressure ventilation is:
o: Whatever volume gives a minimal leak
e: Aim for a leak-free seal at 20–30 cm H2O. Below 20 makes microaspiration more likely; 60 cm H2O is the LMA cuff limit; the minimal leak technique is no longer recommended.

frames.text: Equation of motion: links pressure, volume, flow to compliance & resistance
Pressure must overcome elastic load + resistive load
Asthma = high resistance · ARDS = low compliance → both need more pressure
PC: mechanics change VT & flow · VC: mechanics change pressures
A ventilator controls only one variable at a time: pressure OR volume

q: Per Hess, during volume control, worsening respiratory mechanics change the:
o: Delivered tidal volume and peak flow
Number of variables the ventilator controls
e: During volume control, changes in mechanics affect mean and peak inspiratory pressure. In pressure control they affect peak flow and tidal volume. A ventilator controls only one variable at a time.

frames.text: Absolute humidity = mass of water vapor in a volume of gas (mg/L)
Relative humidity = water content ÷ capacity at that temperature × 100%
Cooler gas, same water content → condensation (rain out)
Humidity deficit = content − 43.8 mg/L (capacity at 37 °C)

q: Relative humidity is defined as:
o: Water content compared with the gas's water capacity at that temperature (× 100%)
Mass of water vapor per liter of gas
e: % Relative humidity = (absolute humidity / humidity capacity) × 100%. Mass of water per liter is absolute humidity; content minus 43.8 mg/L is humidity deficit.

frames.text: PIP = peak pressure; Pplat = end-inspiratory hold (≈ alveolar pressure)
PIP − Pplat = resistive pressure · Pplat − PEEP = elastic (true driving) pressure
Pplat goal: Hess < 30 cm H2O; course slides switch VC → PC if > 30
Another course slide allows Pplat ≤ 30–35 when adjusting VT
PEEP: e.g., 5, 8, 10 cm H2O; PEEP > 10 or PIP > 50 → ↑ barotrauma

q: Per Hess, plateau pressure should ideally be kept:
e: Hess: a high Pplat indicates risk of alveolar overdistention; ideally keep it less than 30 cm H2O. Airway pressures of 50 or more during VC can cause barotrauma.

frames.text: PIP ↑ + Pplat ↑ (gap unchanged) = ↓ compliance (stiff lungs)
PIP ↑ with Pplat unchanged (gap widens) = ↑ airway resistance
↑Raw causes: bronchospasm, secretions, airway edema, plug/kink/biting
Raw improves → opposite changes · Hess: C ↓ fibrosis, edema, atelectasis; ↑ COPD, aging
In PC, worse Raw or compliance shows up as ↓ VT (pressure is fixed)

q: On volume control, PIP rises from 30 to 42 cm H2O while Pplat stays at 22 cm H2O. The most likely problem is:
e: PIP rising with unchanged Pplat widens PIP − Pplat: a resistance problem, such as bronchospasm or secretions. Falling compliance raises both PIP and Pplat.

q: On volume control, PIP and Pplat both rise by the same amount. This suggests:
e: When PIP and Pplat rise together and PIP − Pplat is unchanged, compliance has decreased: think ARDS, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, pneumothorax. Resistance raises PIP alone; a disconnection triggers low-pressure alarms.

frames.text: ↑PEEP/PPV → ↑intrathoracic pressure → ↓venous return → ↓CO → ↓BP
PPV + PEEP: ↑PAP, ↑CVP, ↓aortic pressure, ↓CO
Kidneys: ↓CO → ↓renal perfusion → ↓urine output
PPV ↑ADH and ↓ANF → less urine, fluid retention
Normal UOP: > 400 mL/24 h (deck) · 1 mL/kg/hr (Hess); PEEP can ↑ICP

q: After PEEP is increased, the patient's blood pressure drops. The best explanation is:
o: Higher intrathoracic pressure decreased venous return and cardiac output
PEEP increased venous return, overloading the heart
e: ↑ PEEP → ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ preload → ↓ cardiac output → ↓ BP. PEEP can increase ICP and, with PPV, increase pulmonary artery pressure.

q: Why does urine output often fall during positive pressure ventilation?
o: Lower cardiac output reduces renal perfusion, and ADH increases
Cardiac output rises and causes diuresis
e: PPV lowers cardiac output and renal perfusion; it also increases ADH and reduces ANF, both reducing urine output.

frames.text: Auto-PEEP: unintended trapped pressure at end-exhalation (air trapping)
Spot it: expiratory flow doesn't return to baseline; measure with expiratory hold
At risk: high Raw (COPD, asthma) + modes that limit expiratory time
Fix (more time to exhale): ↓RR, ↑insp flow (VC), ↓VT (VC), ↓Ti (PC)
Harms: hard to trigger (↑WOB), ↓venous return/hypotension, barotrauma

q: A COPD patient on volume control has auto-PEEP. Which change helps reduce it?
e: Auto-PEEP improves with more time to exhale: decrease RR, increase inspiratory flow (VC), decrease VT (VC), or decrease inspiratory time (PC). Raising rate, VT, or I-time does the opposite.

q: Which ventilator graphic finding indicates auto-PEEP?
o: Expiratory flow does not return to baseline before the next breath
Scalloping of the inspiratory pressure waveform
e: Auto-PEEP: expiratory flow does not return to baseline before the next breath. A beak sign means overdistention, and scalloping means inadequate inspiratory flow.

frames.text: Acetylcysteine (NAC, Mucomyst): mucolytic for thick, viscous mucus
Action: free sulfhydryl (thiol) group breaks mucus disulfide bonds
Comes as 10% or 20%; 20% is diluted with normal saline
Hazard: bronchospasm (esp. asthma) → give a bronchodilator before NAC
Airway benefit unproven; antidote for acetaminophen overdose

q: How does acetylcysteine thin mucus?
o: Its sulfhydryl group breaks disulfide bonds in mucoproteins
It digests DNA released from neutrophils
It blocks muscarinic receptors in the airway
e: NAC's free sulfhydryl group breaks disulfide bonds in mucoproteins, lowering viscosity. Digesting neutrophil DNA is dornase alfa; muscarinic blockade is ipratropium; β2 stimulation is albuterol.

q: The main hazard of aerosolized acetylcysteine, especially in asthmatics, is:
e: NAC can trigger bronchospasm, especially in asthmatics, so many clinicians give a bronchodilator before it. Thrush is an inhaled steroid effect; hyperkalemia is a succinylcholine effect; mydriasis is an antimuscarinic effect.

frames.text: Beclomethasone dipropionate (QVAR) = inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)
ICS = maintenance/control of chronic asthma (anti-inflammatory)
Dosed once or twice a day; a prodrug activated in the lung
Side effects: oral thrush, dysphonia → spacer + rinse mouth
High doses: HPA suppression, growth slowing; taper when switching from systemic

q: Beclomethasone dipropionate (QVAR) is best described as:
o: An inhaled corticosteroid for maintenance control of asthma
A short-acting β2 agonist for rescue
e: Beclomethasone dipropionate HFA (QVAR) is an inhaled corticosteroid used for maintenance control of chronic asthma. Albuterol is the rescue SABA; montelukast is a leukotriene antagonist; ipratropium is a SAMA.

q: A patient using an inhaled corticosteroid develops white oral lesions. What reduces this risk?
o: Use a spacer and rinse the mouth after each use
Take the dose right before eating
Stop the ICS abruptly when switching from systemic steroids
e: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) is a common local ICS effect; using a spacer or holding chamber and rinsing the mouth reduces it. Use the minimal dose; high doses raise HPA suppression risk.

frames.text: Albuterol: prototype SABA (β2 agonist) — 'rescue'/'reliever'
β2 stimulation relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation
SABA onset ~15 min, duration 4–6 h
Neb 2.5–5 mg: q20 min in exacerbations, then q1–4 h prn
Side effects: tachycardia, dysrhythmias, tremor, ↓K+, ↑glucose

q: Which side-effect set fits albuterol?
e: β2-agonist systemic effects include tachycardia, dysrhythmias, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and tremor at higher doses. Thrush/dysphonia are ICS effects; fasciculations/hyperkalemia are succinylcholine; dry mouth/mydriasis are antimuscarinic.

frames.text: Levalbuterol (Xopenex) = pure (R)-isomer of albuterol
Racemic albuterol = 50:50 R + S; only R bronchodilates
Hess: ~twice as potent → half the dose; less tachycardia claimed
…but superiority unproven; high doses → same tachyarrhythmias
Neb doses: 0.31, 0.63, 1.25 mg/3 mL, or 1.25 mg/0.5 mL concentrate

q: Levalbuterol differs from albuterol because it is:
e: Levalbuterol (Xopenex) is the pure (R)-isomer of racemic albuterol, a short-acting agent. Racemic albuterol is the 50:50 R/S mixture, and only the R-isomer bronchodilates.

frames.text: Ipratropium (Atrovent) = SAMA: blocks muscarinic ACh receptors
Onset 15 min · peak 1.5 h · lasts up to 6 h
Dosing: MDI 17 µg/puff, 2 puffs QID; neb 0.5 mg QID
Quaternary → stays in lung; most common side effect: dry mouth
With albuterol (DuoNeb 0.5 mg + 2.5 mg): synergistic in COPD; q6h

q: Ipratropium bromide produces bronchodilation by:
e: Ipratropium is a short-acting muscarinic antagonist that blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. β2 stimulation is albuterol; leukotriene blockade is montelukast; breaking disulfide bonds is acetylcysteine.

q: Per the pharmacology deck, ipratropium MDI is dosed as:
e: Ipratropium (Atrovent HFA) MDI: 17 µg/puff, 2 puffs QID; SVN 0.5 mg QID. Once-daily dosing is tiotropium (a LAMA).

frames.text: SABA = rescue/reliever · LABA = maintenance/controller
SABA: onset 15 min, 4–6 h · LABA: onset 20 min, 12–24 h
LABAs: salmeterol, formoterol (~12 h); ultra-LABAs once daily
LABA: never for rescue; never alone in asthma (add to ICS)
LABAs are lipophilic; SABAs are hydrophilic

q: Which drug should NOT be used for quick relief of acute bronchospasm?
e: Salmeterol is a LABA (maintenance controller) and is not intended to replace short-acting β2-agonists for rescue. Albuterol and levalbuterol are rescue SABAs, and the ipratropium/albuterol combination is often dosed more frequently for severe bronchospasm.

q: Per the pharmacology deck, a long-acting β-agonist has an onset and duration of about:
e: Long acting: onset 20 minutes, duration 12 to 24 hours. Short acting (albuterol): onset 15 minutes, 4 to 6 hours. Ultrashort (racemic epinephrine): onset 3-5 minutes, under 3 hours.

frames.text: NMBAs: paralyze skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction
Depolarizing: succinylcholine ONLY — fasciculations, then flaccid paralysis
Sux timing: pharm deck 60–90 s, lasts 10–15 min · Hess 30–60 s, 4–5 min
Sux: hyperkalemia, ↑ICP, ↑intraocular & intragastric pressure, malignant hyperthermia
Nondepolarizing (vecuronium, rocuronium, cisatracurium): competitive; neostigmine reverses
NMBA uses: intubation, vent synchrony, ↓ICP, ↓O2 consumption
On the vent: sedation AND analgesia are absolutely essential
Prolonged paralysis → muscle weakness/atrophy → harder to wean

q: The only depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent is:
e: Succinylcholine is the only depolarizing NMBA. Vecuronium, rocuronium, and cisatracurium are nondepolarizing (competitive) agents.

q: Which statement about reversing neuromuscular blockade is correct?
o: Neostigmine can reverse nondepolarizing agents; nothing reverses succinylcholine
e: Nondepolarizing blockade can be reversed by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as neostigmine; there is no reversal agent for succinylcholine. Naloxone reverses opioids and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

q: A ventilated patient is started on a paralytic. What is absolutely essential?
e: With NMBAs on mechanical ventilation, sedation and analgesia are absolutely essential. Neostigmine reverses blockade, and repeat succinylcholine boluses cause a vagal response.

frames.text: Benzodiazepines (midazolam, lorazepam): GABA → sedation + amnesia
Benzos alone don't change breathing but augment opioid depression
Propofol: lipid, no analgesia; depresses breathing; ↑triglycerides (long/high-dose)
Dexmedetomidine: sedation WITHOUT respiratory depression
RSI agents: etomidate (no analgesia) · ketamine (keeps respiratory drive)

q: Which sedative is unusual because it sedates without causing respiratory depression?
e: Dexmedetomidine provides sedation without respiratory depression. Propofol's respiratory depression limits its use in nonintubated patients; benzodiazepines augment opioid respiratory depression; opioids depress respiratory drive.

frames.text: Opioids (morphine, hydromorphone, fentanyl): ICU analgesia + sedation
All depress respiratory drive (dose-dependent; worse with benzos)
Receptors: mu, delta, kappa
Fentanyl: near-immediate onset, no bolus histamine release · morphine ~5 min
Side effects: constipation, N/V, cough suppression; reverse: naloxone

q: A patient is oversedated after too much morphine. The reversal agent is:
e: Naloxone is the opioid antagonist. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; neostigmine and sugammadex reverse nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade.

q: Benzodiazepines given alone affect breathing how?
o: No change in respiration, but they can augment opioid respiratory depression
e: Benzodiazepines by themselves cause no change in respiration but may augment opioid-induced respiratory depression. Midazolam has no analgesic properties; flumazenil, not naloxone, reverses benzodiazepines.

frames.text: Routes: enteral (GI) · parenteral (injection) · percutaneous/mucosal (incl. inhaled)
Bioavailability: amount reaching systemic circulation vs IV (IV = 100%)
Inhaled: fast, direct to target, skips first-pass liver metabolism
Half-life: time for plasma concentration to fall by half
Metabolism: mainly liver · Elimination: mainly kidney (liver lesser)

q: Bioavailability compares the amount of drug reaching the systemic circulation with which route?
e: Bioavailability refers to the amount of drug available to the systemic circulation as compared to the IV route; an IV dose is said to be 100% bioavailable.

q: What are the main organs of drug metabolism and drug elimination?
e: Metabolism occurs primarily in the liver. The kidney, and to a lesser extent the liver, are the major organs of elimination; lungs, saliva, and sweat are minor routes.

q: A drug's plasma half-life is:
o: The time for its plasma concentration to decrease by one half
The fraction of a dose that reaches the systemic circulation
The time until its peak effect
e: Plasma half-life is the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by one half. The fraction reaching systemic circulation (vs IV) is bioavailability.

frames.text: BUN: protein metabolism + hydration → less specific for kidneys
Creatinine: from muscle; more reliable estimate of GFR
Kidney failure: ↓urine output, ↑BUN, ↑creatinine, ↑K+
Hess normals: BUN 7–21 mg/dL · creatinine 0.7–1.4 mg/dL
Decks differ: BUN 10–20, Cr 0.7–1.5 (principles) · BUN 7–20 (renal deck)

q: Which lab value is the more reliable estimate of GFR (kidney function)?
o: Creatinine, because it comes from muscle and is filtered with minimal reabsorption
BUN, because it is unaffected by diet or hydration
BUN, because it comes from muscle metabolism
Creatinine, because it reflects protein intake and hydration
e: Creatinine comes from muscle metabolism and is filtered at the glomerulus with minimal reabsorption, so it better estimates GFR. BUN reflects protein metabolism and hydration and is less specific.

frames.text: Leukotrienes: potent bronchoconstrictors; edema, mucus, inflammation
Receptor antagonists: montelukast, zafirlukast · 5-LO inhibitor: zileuton
Alternative in mild asthma; add-on with ICS/LABA; not for COPD; modest bronchodilation
Montelukast once daily · zafirlukast twice daily · zileuton IR 4× daily
Zileuton: watch liver enzymes (LFTs)

q: Montelukast (Singulair) works by:
o: Blocking IgE binding to mast cells
e: Montelukast and zafirlukast are leukotriene receptor antagonists. Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase; omalizumab blocks IgE binding; ipratropium blocks muscarinic receptors.

frames.text: IgE drives allergic asthma: mast cells release histamine
Omalizumab (Xolair): IgG monoclonal antibody that blocks IgE
Given subQ every 2–4 weeks; add-on for severe persistent asthma
Most severe risk: anaphylaxis
IL-5 blockers (mepolizumab, benralizumab) for eosinophilic asthma

q: Omalizumab treats allergic asthma by:
o: Binding IgE so it can't attach to mast cells
e: Omalizumab is an IgG monoclonal antibody that inhibits IgE binding to receptors on mast cells and basophils. IL-5 blockers (mepolizumab etc.) treat eosinophilic asthma; montelukast blocks leukotriene receptors.

frames.text: Receptors: β1 = heart · β2 = bronchial smooth muscle · muscarinic = airways
High β2 doses spill onto β1 → tachycardia; M3 block = bronchodilation
Frequency: albuterol MDI q4h prn · ipratropium QID · albuterol/ipratropium q6h
ICS once or twice daily · salmeterol/formoterol ~12 h · tiotropium once daily

q: A patient's heart rate rises after frequent high-dose albuterol. Which receptor is being stimulated?
e: β2 selectivity can be lost when doses are increased or more frequent, causing β1 (cardiac) stimulation and tachycardia. β1 receptors are in cardiac muscle; β2 in bronchial smooth muscle.

q: Which drug is dosed once daily?
e: Tiotropium's prolonged receptor binding allows once-daily dosing. Ipratropium is QID, zafirlukast twice daily, and zileuton immediate-release four times a day.

frames.text: Critical (enters sterile tissue/blood) → STERILIZE
Semicritical (mucous membranes) → high-level disinfection; most RT gear
Noncritical (intact skin) → clean / low-level disinfect
Sterilization kills ALL microbes incl. spores; high-level disinfection may not

q: A reusable bronchoscope contacts the airway mucosa. It is classified and processed as:
e: The bronchoscope contacts mucous membranes, so it is semicritical and needs at least high-level disinfection. Biopsy forceps passed through it into tissue are critical and must be sterilized.

frames.text: Pasteurization = DISINFECTION with hot water (~70 °C for 30 min)
Works like a dishwasher: water just below boiling, then a dryer
Used for heat-sensitive semicritical items (like Cidex/OPA)
Steam autoclave = STERILIZATION (moist heat under pressure)
121 °C for 30 min or 132 °C for 4 min, at 15 psi
Pros: fast, cheap, nontoxic, sporicidal · Con: heat damages some equipment
Heat-sensitive items: ETO, hydrogen peroxide gas plasma, or peracetic acid
Monitor: mechanical, chemical, biological — biological (spores) is best

q: What is the key difference between pasteurization and steam autoclaving?
o: Pasteurization disinfects; the autoclave sterilizes (kills spores)
Pasteurization sterilizes; the autoclave only disinfects
Both sterilize, but pasteurization is faster
Both only clean; neither kills microorganisms
e: Pasteurization disinfects equipment (about 70° C for 30 minutes) and does not kill bacterial spores. Steam autoclaving is the most common sterilization method and is sporicidal; sterilization destroys all microorganisms, including spores.

q: Respiratory equipment is typically pasteurized by immersion in water at about:
e: Pasteurization: about 70° C for 30 minutes. 121° C/30 minutes and 132° C/4 minutes at 15 psi are steam autoclave conditions; 20 minutes at room temperature is glutaraldehyde high-level disinfection.

q: Which provides the strongest verification that a sterilization cycle actually worked?
o: Mechanical readouts of time, temperature, and pressure
e: Biological indicators use highly resistant spores and are the best method for verifying sterilization. Indicator tape shows exposure to the process, and mechanical indicators show the machine ran, but neither proves microorganisms were killed.

frames.text: Isopropyl/ethyl alcohol: skin antiseptic before injections & blood draws
Kills bacteria, TB, fungi, viruses — NOT spores → not for sterilizing
Can damage rubber/plastic; used on stethoscopes, thermometers, vial tops
Alcohol hand rubs are an effective form of hand hygiene

q: Why isn't isopropyl alcohol used to sterilize medical equipment?
o: It leaves a toxic residue like phenolics
e: Alcohols are bactericidal, tuberculocidal, fungicidal, and virucidal, but they do not kill spores, so they are not recommended for sterilizing medical equipment.

frames.text: Chlorhexidine: skin antiseptic before invasive procedures (e.g., A-line)
Course slides: daily chlorhexidine oral care is in the VAP bundle
Hess: chlorhexidine oral care is no longer recommended

q: Per Hess's ventilator-care bundle, oral care with chlorhexidine is:
o: Required daily for every ventilated patient
Recommended only with subglottic suction tubes
e: Hess lists 'Oral care with chlorhexidine (no longer recommended)' and notes it may prove harmful in some patients. Note: the course VAP slide still lists daily chlorhexidine oral care.

frames.text: Glutaraldehyde (Cidex): HLD in 20 min; sterilize 10 h (course) vs 6–10 h (Hess)
After liquid disinfectant: rinse with sterile water
Bleach (hypochlorite) 1:10: blood spills, C. diff rooms; never mix with acid
Quats: noncritical items (BP cuffs, surfaces); not sporicidal; let air dry

q: Per the course slide, glutaraldehyde (Cidex) at room temperature provides high-level disinfection in about ___, but sterilization requires about ___.
e: Course slide: high-level disinfection with glutaraldehyde in 20 minutes at room temperature; true sterilization requires a full 10 hours (Hess: 6 to 10 hours). Always follow the product's instructions.

frames.text: Capnography: exhaled CO2 shown as a number (ETCO2) plus a waveform
Measured by infrared absorption
Mainstream: sensor at the airway → fast; adds weight & dead space
Sidestream: aspirates a sample via tubing; works on cannula; can clog
Setup: confirm inspiratory baseline 0; high calibration uses 5% CO2

q: Which capnometer type can be built into a nasal cannula for a nonintubated patient?
e: Sidestream capnometers can be incorporated into nasal cannula designs for nonintubated patients, and sidestream analyzers can attach to a cannula or mask. Hess: a mainstream sensor is difficult to use with nonintubated patients.

q: A disadvantage of a mainstream capnography sensor is:
o: Added weight on the ETT and extra dead space
Tubing occlusion by water and secretions
It cannot be used on intubated patients
e: Mainstream: fast response, but excessive weight on the ETT and additional dead space. Occlusion of the sampling tube by water and secretions is the sidestream disadvantage.

frames.text: A→B: dead-space gas, no CO2
B→C: CO2 rises (mixed gas) · C→D: alveolar plateau; ETCO2 at end (D)
D→E: inspiration of fresh gas — CO2 drops to zero
Normal ETCO2: course notes give 35–45 mmHg and, elsewhere, 30–43 mmHg
PETCO2 runs 1–5 torr below PaCO2 (more with ↑ dead space)

q: On a normal capnogram, where is PETCO2 measured?
o: At the end of the alveolar plateau (C to D)
At the start of exhalation (A to B)
During the rapid rise (B to C)
e: PETCO2 is typically measured at the end of the alveolar plateau. A to B is dead-space gas with no CO2; B to C is the rise; D to E is inspiration, when CO2 drops to zero.

q: How does PETCO2 normally compare with PaCO2?
o: PETCO2 is 1–5 torr lower, more with high dead space
PETCO2 is about half of PaCO2
e: PETCO2 typically runs 1–5 torr less than PaCO2, more with high dead-space ventilation.

frames.text: Sudden drop to zero → airway/circuit problem first
Baseline doesn't return to zero → rebreathing
'Shark fin' (sloped plateau) → bronchospasm / airway obstruction
Gradual ↑ = hypoventilation (or ↑CO2 production) · gradual ↓ = hyperventilation/↓perfusion
Kinked ETT: PETCO2 falls with the degree of obstruction (0 if complete)

q: The capnogram baseline rises and no longer returns to zero during inspiration. This indicates:
e: An elevated baseline that doesn't return to zero means rebreathing. A shark-fin shape means bronchospasm; a sudden loss of waveform means disconnection; a gradual fall suggests hyperventilation.

q: A "shark-fin" capnogram suggests:
e: Shark fin = airway obstruction/bronchospasm (COPD, asthma, kinked ETT). Rebreathing raises the baseline; esophageal intubation gives a sudden drop to zero; ROSC gives a sudden sustained rise.

frames.text: Sudden ↑ during CPR → ROSC
CPR: PETCO2 < 10 torr = poor/absent pulmonary blood flow
Sudden ↓: cardiac arrest/↓CO or massive PE (lost perfusion)
Sudden ↓: disconnection/leak, esophageal intubation, tube obstruction
Why: ↑ cardiac output → ↑ PETCO₂ · ↓ cardiac output → ↓ PETCO₂

q: During CPR, the PETCO2 suddenly rises and stays up. This most likely indicates:
e: A sudden sustained rise in ETCO2 during CPR can indicate ROSC. Esophageal intubation, massive PE, and disconnection cause sudden decreases.

q: A ventilated patient's ETCO2 waveform suddenly drops to zero. What should you think of FIRST?
o: An airway or circuit problem (disconnection, extubation, obstruction)
e: Sudden drop to zero: think airway/circuit problem first — disconnection, extubation/displacement, esophageal intubation, complete obstruction, equipment failure. Hypoventilation causes a gradual rise; rebreathing raises the baseline.

q: A ventilated patient develops a pulmonary embolism and PETCO2 falls. Should the ventilator rate be reduced?
o: No — the drop reflects dead space, not improved ventilation
Yes — lower PETCO2 means the patient is hyperventilating
e: A decrease in PetCO2 due to dead-space ventilation (e.g., pulmonary embolism) does not mean improved ventilatory status, so the ventilator frequency must not be reduced. Massive PE causes a sudden loss of perfusion and lower PETCO2.

frames.text: IPV: rapid inspiratory pulses; passive exhalation
Air bursts plus aerosol medication
Percussionator: approximately 15–20 minutes; mouthpiece or mask
CF with poor airway clearance: IPV mobilizes mucus
CF: regular airway clearance, individualized choice

q: How does exhalation occur during IPV, according to Hess?
o: Active inspiratory pulses pull gas out
Chest wall elastic recoil provides passive exhalation
e: Hess describes rapid inspiratory flow pulses and passive exhalation through chest wall elastic recoil.

q: Which statement about choosing airway clearance therapy in CF agrees with Hess?
o: IPV has demonstrated superiority over every other method
Airway clearance is unnecessary in CF
All patients must use the same technique regardless of age
Use regular airway clearance and individualize the technique
e: Regular airway clearance is recommended in CF. No therapy has demonstrated superiority; choice should reflect age, preference, and adverse events.

q: Hess describes approximately how long a Percussionator treatment lasts?
e: Hess specifies approximately 15 to 20 minutes for the Percussionator, used with a mouthpiece or mask.

frames.text: Inhaled NO: selective pulmonary vasodilation
Hess: approved for term/near-term neonates >34 weeks
Improves oxygenation; reduces need for ECMO
ARDS use is off-label
ARDS: temporary oxygenation improvement; no demonstrated mortality benefit
NO + O2 → NO2: airway reactivity and lung injury
Methemoglobin: monitor with CO-oximetry
Other risks: renal dysfunction and inhibited platelet function
Withdrawal: rebound hypoxemia and pulmonary hypertension

q: Which population matches Hess’s approved INOmax indication?
o: All premature neonates, regardless of gestation or oxygenation
Adults with ARDS as routine mortality-reducing therapy
Term/near-term neonates >34 weeks with hypoxic respiratory failure and pulmonary hypertension
All children with hypoxemia, regardless of pulmonary pressure
e: Hess specifies term/near-term neonates >34 weeks with hypoxic respiratory failure and pulmonary hypertension, with ventilatory support. Other uses are off-label.

q: What does Hess report about inhaled NO in ARDS?
o: It may initially improve oxygenation, without demonstrated mortality benefit
ARDS is the only FDA-approved indication
e: The initial PaO2 improvement is lost after several days, and trials failed to show improved mortality. The approved indication is neonatal; ARDS use is off-label.

q: What can happen after inhaled NO is discontinued?
o: Hypoxemia and pulmonary hypertension may worsen
Rebound is limited to improved oxygenation
e: Hess describes rebound hypoxemia and pulmonary hypertension after discontinuation, sometimes leading to hemodynamic instability.

q: During INO delivery, how do the course slides say to assess metHb?
o: CO-oximetry every 4–6 hours, according to protocol and dose
No monitoring is needed at therapeutic doses
e: The slides specify CO-oximetry at 4- to 6-hour intervals, according to institutional protocol and delivered dose.

frames.text: P–V slope falls → compliance falls
P–V slope rises → compliance rises
Vent-deck resistance notes: wider P–V loop = higher resistance
Conflict: the same deck’s X-Y loop slide says thinner = more resistance
Flow–volume loop: narrow expiratory limb = higher resistance
Increased inspiratory resistance: inspiratory limb shifts right
Course slides: beak beyond UIP → overdistension
Slides: UIP means overdistension; Hess: may mark end of recruitment
Course slides: set PEEP just above the lower inflection point
Hess: pressure-control loops cannot identify optimal PEEP or VT
Flow–volume: check the display’s expiratory-flow orientation
Higher resistance → lower peak expiratory flow
Bronchodilator response: improved peak expiratory flow
Sawtooth pattern: excessive airway secretions
Open or broken loops: check for a leak
Correct the leak → loops return to normal shape
Auto-PEEP clue: expiratory flow persists on the flow–time scalar

q: Per the course slides, a decreased pressure–volume slope indicates:
o: Lower compliance and a stiffer respiratory system
e: A decreased slope indicates decreased compliance and a stiffer respiratory system.

q: Per the course vent deck’s resistance-graph notes, how does increased inspiratory resistance change the P–V loop?
o: The inspiratory limb shifts to the left
The inspiratory limb shifts to the right
A beak appears beyond the upper inflection point
The loop shifts toward the volume axis
e: The notes say the inspiratory limb shifts right: more pressure is needed to deliver the same volume, as with bronchospasm, kinked tubing, or secretions.

q: In the course slides, the beak beyond the upper inflection point indicates:
o: Optimal PEEP at the lower inflection point
e: The slides identify the beak as overdistention with excessive VT. Hess qualifies UIP interpretation: it might mark the end of recruitment.

q: On a flow–volume loop, what pattern does Hess associate with excessive airway secretions?
o: Sawtooth on inspiratory and expiratory curves
e: Hess describes excessive secretions producing sawtooth patterns on both inspiratory and expiratory flow–volume curves.

q: Per the waveform deck, which pattern suggests a circuit or airway leak?
o: A closed loop with equal inspired and expired volume
An open loop with expired volume less than inspired volume
A loop with expired volume always greater than inspired volume
No change in loop closure or measured volume
e: The deck describes broken/open loops and expiratory volume less than inspiratory volume with leaks in the circuit or around the ETT/trach.

q: Per the waveform deck, reduced airway resistance should change peak expiratory flow how?
e: Decreased resistance produces higher peak expiratory flow; increased resistance produces lower peak expiratory flow.

frames.text: Placement: well-perfused chest side, abdomen, or inner thigh
Gel without bubbles; sensor flat; edges sealed
Usually 44°C for both gases; as low as 37°C for CO2 alone
Change sites to avoid burns: follow device and patient factors
Calibration failure: leaking membrane or trapped air
Adhesive-ring air leak: PtcCO2 falls dramatically
Large leak: PO2 ≈150 torr, PCO2 ≈0 torr; replace adhesive ring
Low PtcO2: check perfusion, heat, site, pressure, and gel
Shock or poor peripheral circulation: avoid transcutaneous monitoring
Need precision? Compare with simultaneous arterial PO2

q: Which transcutaneous sensor placement follows the course procedure?
o: A bony surface under firm pressure
A well-perfused site on the chest side, abdomen, or inner thigh
A site selected without regard to superficial circulation
e: Choose good superficial circulation, such as the side of the chest, abdomen, or inner thigh. Bony placement or excessive pressure can underestimate PaO2.

q: A large adhesive-ring leak makes transcutaneous readings resemble which gas values?
e: The course slide gives room-air-like readings: PO2 approximately 150 torr, PCO2 approximately 0 torr. Reapply the sensor using a new adhesive ring.

q: The transcutaneous monitor fails calibration. Which explanation is listed in the course slides?
o: A properly sealed, intact membrane with no trapped air
A successful calibration with precision gases
A stabilized reading from a flat sensor
A leaking membrane or excessive air trapped under the membrane
e: Calibration failure is usually due to a leaking membrane or excessive trapped air beneath it.

q: When precision is needed, how should PtcO2 be checked?

Use a nonsimultaneous value regardless of condition

e: The respiratory-effort row assigns 0 for none, 1 for weak/irregular effort, and 2 for a strong cry.

It replaces visual assessment of the patient

Methylxanthine treatment at home excludes monitoring
Risk of central apnea excludes monitoring

o: PaO2 alone from a standard ABG
A calculated saturation from a standard ABG alone

e: Glasgow assesses impaired consciousness using eye-opening, motor, and verbal responses.

q: Which assessment estimates newborn gestational age from neuromuscular and physical maturity?
e: Ballard evaluates neuromuscular and physical maturity to estimate newborn gestational age.

q: Which score assesses infant respiratory distress, with a higher score indicating greater distress?
e: Silverman assesses infant respiratory distress; a higher score means greater distress.

q: For which score does a HIGHER number mean the patient is doing WORSE?
e: Silverman: the higher the score, the greater the distress. Apgar 7–10 is normal and GCS 15 is fully alert (higher is better); a higher Ballard score means a higher gestational age.

q: What is the range of the total Glasgow Coma Scale score?
e: GCS runs from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully alert). 0 to 10 is the Apgar range.

q: Per the course, a GCS of 8 or less indicates:
e: Severe impairment (coma): ≤ 8 (GCS ≤ 8 = Intubate!). Moderate is 9–12; mild is 13–15.

q: Per Hess, a New Ballard score of 40 corresponds to:
e: A normal score of 40 corresponds to 40 weeks’ gestation; less than 40 is preterm, greater than 40 is post-term.

q: Per the course example, 40% FiO2 with 10 L/min oxygen input gives what TOTAL flow?
e: The ratio is 3:1. Add 3 + 1 = 4, then multiply 4 × 10 = 40 L/min total.

e: The ratio remains 3:1. Add 3 + 1 = 4, then multiply 4 × 5 = 20 L/min total.

e: Course: pt on 10 lpm @ 60% FiO2, ratio 1:1 (add 1 + 1 = 2). 3:1 is the 40% ratio.

q: Per the course, what total flow is the best way to ensure a stable FiO2?
e: The best way to ensure a stable FiO2 is to provide a total flow of at least 40 L/min.
